#3482. This Year, Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Is Doing Broadway a Little Differently

This year’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is going to look a bit different. First, the threat of severe weather has prompted Macy’s to reschedule the event until Saturday, beginning at 8:30 a.m. ET. But even before the forecast turned, there was a big change: While in the past, viewers would enjoy five or so of the best performances from the current Broadway season, this year, there’s only one big Broadway number. But don’t fret, theater folk. For the milestone occasion of the parade’s 100th anniversary, the powers that be at NBC and Macy’s have put a new spin on their tried-and-true formula, gathering the Broadway community for one supersized performance, featuring more shows and performers than ever before.

The result is an epic 10-minute medley, introduced by Julianne Hough, who will star in Damn Yankees on Broadway this spring, featuring nine beloved Broadway shows: The Book of Mormon, Chicago, Disney’s Aladdin, Hamilton, The Lost Boys, Rent, Richard O’Brien’s The Rocky Horror Show, Schmigadoon!, and—what else?—Wicked.

The mastermind behind the mega-medley is none other than Tom Kitt, the Tony-, Emmy-, Grammy-, and Pulitzer Prize–winning composer behind Next to Normal, If/Then, and Almost Famous. Kitt is no stranger to writing a big production number, having cowritten the Tony Awards opening number “Bigger!,” performed by host Neil Patrick Harris with lyrics by Lin-Manuel Miranda in 2013, among other ambitious musical endeavors. Despite his previous experience, a 10-minute, nine-show medley presented a unique set of challenges the composer had yet to tackle.

A total of 133 people are performing in the medley—114 Broadway cast members, 17 dancers, a child actor, and Hough. On top of that, more than 125 other Broadway professionals—including stage managers, wardrobe supervisors, and hair and makeup teams—are on site to facilitate the production, bringing the total number of people involved to well over 250.

“Most important to me in doing something like this—to celebrate this community, this beautiful community that I’m so lucky to be a part of,” Kitt tells me. “Everyone who’s participating, you want them to feel happy and excited about what they’re doing.”

A little over a month ago, Kitt and creative producer Sarah O’Gleby got to work figuring out how to make a cohesive musical number out of nine very different shows. He wrote the first draft of the arrangement over the course of a few days. “It was way too long,” he says. That might be because Kitt had to figure out how to connect these disparate shows musically while also finding room for Easter eggs for theater fans: musical nods to shows that might not otherwise be featured in the medley, including Anything Goes, The Music Man, A Chorus Line, and Kitt’s personal favorite, Into the Woods, whose music kicks things off.

“Into the Woods was one of those shows that made me want to write for the theater,” he tells me. “The downbeat of the prologue is one of the most beautiful musical gestures; every time I hear it, I get goosebumps. So that was really special and important for me to get to plug into, and there are so many others.”

Surprisingly, it will be Kitt’s first time attending the parade in person. “The parade has meant so much to me,” he says. “I’ve watched it for years. I’ve taped it. I’m lucky enough to have shows that have been a part of it. I think that celebrating that relationship and celebrating the history of Broadway and being able to spotlight so many important shows and artists just feels very exciting and gratifying.”

“I’m a tiny little person, but I love to do really big things,” says O’Gleby. A former performer on the West End, O’Gleby moved to the States almost two decades ago to pursue a career as a Broadway performer, dancing in revivals of Brigadoon and How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying. Now she choreographs Broadway productions like Shucked and, most recently, Pink’s widely celebrated Tony Awards opening number. Given her Broadway bona fides, she’s also intimately familiar with the magic of the parade. “I was lucky to perform on the parade as a Broadway girl and the associate choreographer and dance captain on shows that I was in,” she says. “It was so wonderfully American.”

The first of two rehearsals took place Friday afternoon at Pier59 Studios at Chelsea Piers. Around 4 p.m., as the sun began to set over the Hudson River, Broadway performers from different shows practiced the medley. O’Gleby, wearing silver leather pants and clutching a God mic, was charged with organizing the chaos and managing the more than 100 Broadway performers in the room. Standing offstage between a broomstick and a red Les Mis flag, I could still see traces of green makeup on the face of Wicked’s current Elphaba, Keri René Fuller. Most of the performers gathered had a show of their own to perform in just a few hours, but that didn’t stop them from giving it their all in rehearsal, onstage and off, cheering the other productions along as each got its moment in the spotlight.

Case in point: At the end of the rehearsal, the whole room erupted into cheers for the original cast members from Rent—including original Angel, Tony winner Wilson Jermaine Heredia, and original Joanne, Fredi Walker—who are gathering to perform “Seasons of Love” in the parade. (During the rehearsal, Aladdin’s current Genie, Sherri Shepherd, couldn’t help but mouth along to the words of the seminal song.) “It was that moment of why we’re a part of this community,” O’Gleby says, nearly choking up. “Everyone in the room—stage managers, costume, I mean everybody in the room—the way they were applauding these original cast members and what they gave to all of us as a community, really all over the world, it was incredible.”

At the second rehearsal, on Monday night outside on 34th Street beneath Macy’s giant turkey, the mood remained high even as the temperatures dropped. By 11 p.m., performers were bundled in winter jackets, sweatshirts, and leg warmers, with their character shoes still on. They hugged one another for warmth and jumped up and down, kicking their feet to stay loose between setups. Margaret Cho, who stars as the Narrator in The Rocky Horror Show, danced “The Time Warp” with her Chihuahua, Lucia, tucked into a pouch in her jacket, the dog’s head peeking out.

For O’Gleby, a smooth Monday-night rehearsal means setting each show up for success come Saturday morning and making sure all nine shows are “represented in the most powerful and clear storytelling way that we can,” she says. “This is a huge moment for these shows to sell lots of tickets so everyone gets to keep making their magic every night. And so it’s important to me that each team gets to communicate what they need and what they think would really make their show shine.”

On Wednesday afternoon, Macy's announced that “after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” a disappointing piece of news for those who build their holiday around the annual event.

This is only the fourth time in history that the parade hasn't been held on Thanksgiving: In 1942, 1943, and 1944 it was canceled completely as its trademark giant balloons were repurposed as part of the World War II effort. Compared to those years, a move to Saturday seems manageable, O’Gleby says. “The weather will be what it will be, but we will delight in that and deliver the best."

Prices start at $299 for the compact Nebula P1i and go up to $2,799 for the premium X1S 4K laser projector, with savings of up to $700 across the models we've rounded up. There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

The Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and shows. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

#3480. New Dungeon Crawler Carl Release Officially Set for 2027

Matt Dinniman's massive LitRPG series continues to grow

Even if you haven't read any of the books, you've probably heard of Dungeon Crawler Carl at this point. The LitRPG book series (a genre defined by its use of video game and tabletop RPG mechanics) by Matt Dinniman has become a cultural juggernaut, and it is only getting bigger. In addition to a television adaptation, Dungeon Crawler Carl is also getting another new adaptation in 2027.

Vault Comics will be publishing an ongoing Dungeon Crawler Carl comic. The new comic will serialize the existing webtoon adaptation of Dungeon Crawler Carl, retaining writer Tevagah with artwork by Laurel Pursuit Studios. Kuzomari will also join the series to help adapt the art to the larger comic-book format. Nathan Gooden will provide the main covers, with plenty of variants also being made available.

For the uninitiated, this is the official synopsis for the series:

Dungeon Crawler Carl follows Coast Guard vet Carl and his ex-girlfriend’s cat, Princess Donut, as they try to survive the end of the world — or just get to the next level — in a video game-like, trap-filled fantasy dungeon. A dungeon that’s actually the set of a reality television show with countless viewers across the galaxy.

On the latest adaptation of his novels, Dinniman said, "Entering the comic space is nothing short of amazing. The fact that I get to work with some of the greatest creators and artists working today feels like a dream.”

The first issue of the Dungeon Crawler Carl comic will be a double-sized, 48-page affair and is set to be released in January 2027.

We know Dinniman is actively working on the ninth book in the series, though there is no release date as of yet. It is currently being called The Beautiful Place, and the author has even shared the prologue and early chapters. The most recent book in the series was released this year, and if Dinniman writes at his usual pace, it wouldn't be unsurprising to see the ninth book release sometime in late 2027. Dinniman has said this will begin the conclusion to the series, which should end with the tenth book.

Beyond the main series, a lot of Dungeon Crawler Carl projects are still in the works. During New York Comic Con, Universal Global Television scripted series chief Kelsey Balance revealed that shooting could begin as early as next year. Dungeon Crawler Carl also has a pretty solid tabletop RPG.

Matt Dinniman’s hit LitRPG series moves forward, with more details expected very soon

#3479. Steve Martin And John Candy's Classic Thanksgiving Movie Is A Paramount+ Streaming Hit

John Hughes made some of the most beloved movies of all time in his eight directorial efforts, to the point where it's nearly impossible to rank the films he wrote and directed. Still, there are few movies that reach the specific balance of comedy with such an emotional punch as Hughes does in 1987's "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." This is a goofball movie that borders on the surreal, with some of the most bizarre imagery in a comedy movie, while also delivering some of the most heartbreaking and heartwarming moments that came out of the 1980s.

The film stars Steve Martin as Neal Page, an uptight marketing executive forced to be paired with Del Griffith (John Candy), a goofball salesman with a heart of gold, when their journey from New York City to Chicago is disrupted. What was meant to be just a short cab and plane ride home just in time for Thanksgiving ends up being a three-day odyssey full of shenanigans, attempted murder, and much more.

It's no wonder, then, that "Planes, Trains and Automobiles" is the No. 1 movie streaming on Paramount+ on Thanksgiving Day 2026. After all, there are plenty of movies about Christmas, to the point where it's easy to overlook Thanksgiving, and with good reason. For one, it's not really a holiday outside the U.S. and Canada (and even then, celebrated on different days), and the imagery is not dissimilar to Christmas anyway. Still, the best Thanksgiving movies deliver a very specific tone that's less about holiday magic and more about celebrating what we have despite the horrors of daily life. From the opening minutes of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles," it's clear this movie could not be set at any other time of year except during the chaos and anxiety of Thanksgiving.

The travel chaos that is quite unique to Thanksgiving is the crux of "Planes, Trains and Automobiles." The arrival of snowstorms that plague the East Coast of the continental United States, the huge flux of travelers, and the general anxiety and irritability of travelers around the country add to, well, a very stressful time of year. It's why Steve Martin's uptight businessman Neal is so relatable. The film simply nails the feeling of needing to interact with others and ask for their help while being utterly frustrated with having to deal with anyone at such a bad time. It's also why John Candy's performance is such a tightrope, because his character has to be annoying in addition to being charming. Del's not really someone you'd want as a travel companion, yet he is absolutely the best person you want as a friend.

That tricky balance is what makes the movie so memorable, and why John Candy's best line remains the best Thanksgiving movie quote ever. Neal and Del are forced to not only set aside their differences, but actually recognize the humanity in each other while acknowledging that they themselves are flawed. This is a highly empathetic film that's all about how we should find love and camaraderie even in unlikely companions. That is why the film so perfectly captures the spirit of Thanksgiving, because it's not about estranged family members, but rather complete strangers who must come to learn they need one another and that they should be grateful for what they bring into each other's lives. Togetherness is not just for family members, or even people you like, but also for strangers you come to appreciate despite the ways they annoy you.

Supernatural may have ended over six years ago, but the series is still a fan-favorite when it comes to rewatches with your Peacock subscription. The show’s 15 seasons were a roller coaster ride involving the Winchester brothers fighting just about everything Hell would throw at them, and more. However, Supernatural’s controversial series finale has given fans a lot to talk about, and a lot of it is not great. After hearing Jensen Ackles’ own version of the ending, I wish we had gotten that instead.

The Supernatural series finale in November 2020 saw Ackles’ Dean getting killed while on a hunt and Sam (Jared Padalecki) living the rest of his life with an unknown wife and a son who was named after his brother. Sam eventually died of old age and met back up with Dean in Heaven. It’s been previously revealed the SPN finale was very different pre-COVID, and a lot of it changed and people had to be cut out, understandably.

Ackles reiterated what the ending would have been had it not been for COVID while at a Supernatural fan convention ( via tvdkami), and I am once again mourning what the pandemic took from us:

Loved to have actually gotten to shoot the ending that we were intending to shoot. That being said, that doesn’t change the outcome of how it ended. So if we got to do the ending that was originally scripted, which I think a lot of you know, and for those that don’t, was Sam comes to Heaven and walks up to The Roadhouse, and I come out, and we have that little meeting that we ended up having on the bridge.

I would have loved more than anything for this to actually happen. The amount of characters that Supernatural introduced and killed off during its run, or just straight-up forgot about, was a large number. He went on to talk about Kansas performing, a moment that would have been absolutely perfect, given that “Carry On Wayward Son” was SPN’s unofficial theme song. It would have looked like this:

But then I say, ‘Hey, come in here. Some people I want you to see.’ We walk through The Roadhouse, it’s all the people from the show, all the characters. The actual band Kansas was going to be the ‘Roadhouse band.’ And then they were signed on to do it. I think one of them was on a plane about to head to Vancouver when they got the call and said, ‘Hey, we’re shutting down. Get off the plane.’

Of course, there is only so much that could have been done at the time with all the restrictions, and at the very least, the series brought back Jim Beaver as Sam and Dean’s late surrogate father, Bobby Singer. That was better than nothing, in my opinion.

There were a lot of expectations for Supernatural's finale, and it's still disappointing to think about, even considering the extenuating circumstances. That hasn't stopped Ackles from sharing his own take about what he would have done with the finale.

For him, he also feels like there was a missed opportunity to end the show on a twist, something Supernatural was known for doing.

So I would have liked for that to happen, but I’ll add just a little extra to that, which is during that kind of reunion, so to speak, I would have liked Jack to come through the front door and just walk up to Sam and Dean and be like, ‘I need to send you guys back.’ And then that’s the end. Then we’re just like, ‘What? Well, wait!’ Which just would have been great, which just opens the door right to something into the future. We can still do it. Not too late. But, by the way, we could go back to that bridge and be just looking out and pull back, and Jack’s behind us, and he’s like, ‘Guys, I hate to do this to you.’

I would have been alright with an ending like this, despite it's shocking nature. Though I'll admit it's mostly because I wasn’t fond of how the finale turned out. Dean’s death dragged on, the penultimate felt more like a finale with how Sam, Dean and Jack defeated God/Chuck, and Castiel dying. Yes, things could and should have been different and they worked with what they had, but I still wish it had played out in a different manner.

Having recently rewatched Supernatural, I saw the finale again, and definitely think it could have been better. However, I’m just glad the series was able to still knock out a finale given the circumstances, and we can still extrapolate out all of this stuff from the cast in hindsight. Could have, should have, would have.

#3477. The Latest Apple Watch Is Up to $100 Off for Black Friday

Apple's latest flagship smartwatch, the Apple Watch Series 12, is worth the upgrade. With this model, Apple has upgraded the processor, added a new heart rate sensor, and improved the display durability. It's certainly one of Apple's best smartwatches, but that also means it isn't cheap: All these new features give the new Series 12 a starting price of $399, which only increases if you choose a model with cellular data. However, for Black Friday, you can take up to $100 off the Series 12, bringing the starting price down to $299.

The three biggest hardware upgrades with the Apple Watch Series 12 are the heart rate sensor, the S11 chip, and Ceramic Shield 2. That heart rate sensor now checks your pulse every five seconds, or 20 times a minute. Apple says the Series 12 checks your heart rate variability 24 times more than the Series 11, and your background heart rate 60 times more frequently than the Series 11. The company is even so bold as to say the Series 12 has the most accurate heart rate monitor on a wearable.

Powering the new heart rate monitor is the S11 chip, Apple's latest processor for the Apple Watch. The S11 isn't only responsible for these new heart rate features, however. In addition to running the same watchOS 27 features as other compatible Apple Watches, the S11 on the Series 12 can run Audio Intelligence, Apple's new suite of AI-powered audio features. That includes "Live Rewind," which lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation, and "Siri Recaps," which displays summaries of your conversations throughout the day. Finally, the other major advantage with the Series 12 is Ceramic Shield 2. This is a display upgrade that Apple typically reserves for more premium Apple Watch finishes, but this year, the aluminum Series 12 gets it as well. That means the watch should be more durable against scratches and cracks, without you having to upgrade to the more expensive model.

How much you'll save on a Series 12 depends on the size, color, and model. At this time, Amazon is selling certain colors of the 42mm Series 12 for $299, while certain colors of the 46mm option run $449 (also marked down by $100). You can also save on the cellular models as well: The 42mm option is currently $429 (down from $499), while the 46mm model is $449 (down from $549).

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3476. Kerry Kennedy on Her Brother RFK Jr.: “We Were Very Close, but He Changed”

Kerry Kennedy is not in Milan on political business, but it’s hard to rein in the enthusiasm of some Americans following the 2026 midterm elections. Democrats won decisive majorities in both the House and Senate, along with 24 of the 36 governors elections held this month. It was a blue tsunami. Kennedy—a lawyer and human rights activist born in 1959 to dynasty Democrats Robert and Ethel Kennedy—is in a celebratory mood.

She’s in town for one night only to attend a charity dinner in support of her foundation, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. But first she sits down with Vanity Fair Italia, and over the course of our chat, she takes her beloved poodle, Scamper, for a short walk; sips two cappuccinos (strictly decaf), one of them iced (she apologizes to the Italians present); eats some gianduiotti chocolates; gestures animatedly; and smooths her very blonde hair.

But above all, she never stops smiling: “In America you can only go so far in the attempt to avoid the rule of law and erode democracy,” she says, making clear that her political statements are delivered in her personal capacity, “because at a certain point, even if you’re the most powerful and the richest man there, democracy will bring you down. [The president] made a mess all over the world, but in the end, in America, democracy was stronger.”

From left: Robert Kennedy Jr., Joseph P Kennedy Jr., Tory Kennedy, and Kerry Kennedy on January 1, 1994

Kerry Kennedy: They’re upset about high prices. And they don’t like the corruption.

What do you think will happen to Donald Trump and his associates?

I think that [Representative] Jamie Raskin is now going to be the head of the Judiciary Committee. I happen to know him very, very, very well because Jamie and I studied for the bar together. He’s brilliant, he’s determined, and he hates anything that harms our Constitution. I think that Trump is going to face impeachment. The rumors are that Trump’s going to fire [Pete] Hegseth, but if he isn’t fired, he’ll certainly be impeached.

What will be the repercussions of the blue tsunami for Tehran?

Iran’s leader at the moment, [Mojtaba Khamenei], has seen his father murdered by Trump. His head of state was murdered by Trump. His spiritual leader was murdered by Trump. Now Trump wants to make a peace deal with this guy. The only way to make progress is for the Iranians to think that it’s not Trump but someone else who’s negotiating.

The fact that Donald Trump sold out Western values in Ukraine for a barrel of oil from a mad, thieving, murderous dictator in Russia shocked the American people and shocked people around the world. Congress has the power of the purse, and now it’s going to exercise that power. But…

He’s still the president for two more years. We didn’t get the White House.

Ethel Kennedy and daughter Kerry Kennedy circa 1979

Who is your ideal candidate for the 2028 presidential election?

Do you think [President Barack] Obama played a role in the Democrats’ success?

Obama is beloved. The only person who’s beloved more is Michelle [Obama]. And when I watched his speeches, he was so clear and concise about the differences between the Republicans and the Democrats, with his moral authority and his joy.

You’ve talked about how your mother supported your father. Can you share an example of that?

My father was working for the Senate, and he was investigating organized crime’s infiltration of the Teamsters union, stealing pension funds from the rank-and-file Teamsters. There was a journalist from the New York Post who was also investigating, and somebody threw acid in his face. He was permanently blinded. A few days later, my mother got an anonymous letter saying, “Your children will be next.” She took her three oldest kids, put them in the back of her car, drove them to the Capitol, walked into the hearing room, and sat in the front row while daddy was interrogating Jimmy Hoffa, the head of the Teamsters.

She was saying, “You’re not going to get to me through my children, and you’re not going to get to my husband through me. We are a fortress and we’re coming after you.” I don’t know how she grappled with the trauma.

She needed to be there for us. She was an athlete. And if you feel physically mighty, it’s very helpful when you have to also be psychologically mighty. She would get up and go swimming, then horseback riding, sailing, and after a sail, she would go for a swim. She also had a very deep faith. She went to Mass every day, prayed before and after every meal, and she made us read the Bible out loud at the dinner table every night.

Yes. In December, I’ll step down from being president of this organization. I’ll stay on the board and I’ll be president emeritus and I’ll still be involved, but I want to go to divinity school.

Stephen Colbert and Kerry Kennedy on December 11, 2013

I don’t know. I have to apply and be accepted.

In 2008 you wrote the bestseller Being Catholic Now. What does it mean to be Catholic in 2026?

For Americans, we have had this extremely disruptive, terrifying time for the last two years, and there are existential threats that everybody in the world is facing. And suddenly there’s an American pope who’s saying, “When you feel this is wrong, it is wrong. When this president is allowing ICE agents to go into American cities and start shooting people, that’s wrong. We need to have compassion toward one another. We need to have love toward one another. Every human being is valuable.”

He’s one of the few voices—not one Republican senator has stood up, and other leaders around the world really have not stood up. Mark Carney did from Canada.

Pedro Sánchez [Spain’s prime minister] did a little bit.

Yes, but not much. The pope has been the main person, and I think that’s renewed people’s faith because it’s very simple as a political leader to call on people’s anger and hatred and fury. It’s a simple trick to get elected. But what people really want you to do in the end is call upon their better angels and say, “You’re good. I see that the God in me sees the God in you.” That is the alternative message, and that’s the spiritual message. I think that it’s created a revival of faith. My daughter Cara is 31 years old, and every Sunday night, she and all of her friends go to church and it’s packed.

What lesson did you learn from your parents?

When we were kids, when we would have a battle, and there were lots of battles, my father always did the same thing. He would bring two of us into a room. My brother had to be silent, and I would tell my father what happened and all the horrible things my brother did. And then I’d have to be silent, and he would tell his story. And then it would be clear that neither of us was completely innocent. We would have to kiss and make up and go to our rooms to read for an hour. His message to us was his message to our country, which is: You have to stop thinking of your adversary as your enemy and think of them as your brother and sister.

Your brother, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., currently the secretary of health in the Trump administration, is known for his anti-vax views. You’ve often said, “I love him very much, but I don’t agree with him.”

We were very close, but he changed and went way over there. And that’s where he is today. But we have much more in common than not.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr and Kerry Kennedy on May 20, 2015

I’m not going to go talk to him about vaccine policy. That’s not going to change him, and he’s not going to change me. So when I’m with him, I want to talk about, how are his animals? How are his children? His daughter, who is my goddaughter, Kyra, lives here in Milan, and she’s getting married to an Italian, and I’m so happy for her. There are many things to talk about besides vaccines.

Your shared past also includes the assassination of your father. Who told you that news?

We were all together in the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles and we were watching the returns, but I was eight and I went to sleep. I woke up very early the next morning because I was still on East Coast time, and I went into the living room area of my hotel room. I turned on the TV to watch Bugs Bunny. That’s how I learned.

Did you guys see a therapist when you were little?

Of course not. It was 1968. If it happened today, every kid would get their own therapist; back then, you dealt with it.

Other students were reading Charlotte’s Web, and I was trying to figure out if somebody was going to kill someone in my family. What happens if Mommy dies? Are they going to split us up? Who could take 11 kids? Houses aren’t big. Where do we go? Would we see each other on Christmas?

Were you a happy little girl before that day?

When I was a child, my parents really didn’t separate my father’s life and work from our home. So Daddy would call my mother and say, “You know what? There are three or four of us. We’re trying to work out this [policy] issue. Could we come home for lunch?” Sure. And then he’d call back half an hour later. “Actually, now we’re 12.”

They sat at the dining room table, and there would be three or four kids doing homework and eating peanut butter and jelly sandwiches and asking them to pass the milk. And then they would be talking about these issues. My mother would come in and say, “Time to play football.” And everybody would get up and go out. For us kids, it felt like we were part of something bigger.

Your latest book, which has just been published, is a biography of your mother: Ethel Kennedy: The Extraordinary Life and Bold Legacy. What kind of person was she?

My mother loved men. If you’re a woman, you’re great, and you’re her friend. But when a man was watching, it was incredible. Her whole life, that’s the way she was. When she was 96 and her mind was kind of in and out, I called her from my hotel in Milan and I said, “I’m here. Can I bring you anything? Do you want some limoncello or a bag of that beautiful spaghetti that they sell at the airport? What can I bring you from Italy?” And she answered, “An Italian boyfriend would be nice.”

Now, Prime Video is getting in on the fun with the release of Clashing Through the Snow. As of writing this, the festive flick is sitting in the number three spot on the streamer’s trending charts, but don’t let the popularity fool you. Some fans are really upset that the film featured a character asking ChatGPT for relationship advice, and I agree with their outrage.

The romantic comedy follows rival book editors Hannah (Michelle Randolph) and Ryan (Christopher Briney) who, after learning their jobs were in jeopardy unless they could wow their boss, set out to land major book deals. When weather and a series of misfortunes halt their respective travel plans, the two begrudgingly agree to road trip to New York together. The proximity allows them to bond, and sparks start to fly, complicating their career ambitions.

Clashing Through the Snow is overflowing with witty banter, memorable scenes, and hilarious and endearing side characters, which is why it was so upsetting when Ryan opted to ask ChatGPT for relationship advice instead of calling his friend Walter (Andrew Schulz), who had already given him advice earlier in the film.

Fans were not happy with the unexpected turn and quickly turned to Twitter to air their grievances over the egregious use of AI:

Things weren’t much better over on Threads, where fans also made their distaste for the inclusion abundantly clear:

I don’t know what’s more upsetting: the fact that the film had a Ryan ask ChatGPT for advice or the fact that he was a senior book editor with human friends he could have turned to.

What might be the most infuriating thing is that apparently there was a version of Clashing through the Snow where Ryan did turn to a human instead of ChatGPT. At least that’s what Carlson Young, the film’s director, told Deadline before defending her decision to go with the scene in the film, saying:

I personally thought that him talking to Chat was so Ryan. It made me laugh so much. And the amount of times that I’ve caught my husband… I’m like, ‘Are you asking ChatGPT a question? Like for real? Are you serious? ‘And he is serious. It just felt really modern and so of the times, and something like his character would actually do. And I like a lot the responses that Chat has for him. It just made me laugh.

Maybe I missed something, but I can’t wrap my head around hopeless romantic, pragmatic Ryan being the character who would turn to ChatGPT to ask for serious relationship help. That seems like a job he would have wanted a human who can experience actual love to help with, like Walter or even some random stranger he could have stumbled upon.

As upsetting as it is to see an amazing character turn to AI for help, I don’t think one scene should tarnish the rest of the movie. Clashing Through the Snow is a swoonworthy and hilarious rom-com that does deserve its flowers. Dare I say it might be Briney's best rom-com role (yes, even better than his portrayal as Conrad Fisher in The Summer I Turned Pretty).

Clashing Through the Snow is streaming now for those with an active Prime Video subscription.

#3474. 30 Years Later, Jingle All The Way's Funniest Line Is Still The Best Christmas Movie Quote

There are classic Christmas movies like "It's a Wonderful Life" and "National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation," and then there are the Christmas movies that we just watch every year because they're on repeatedly, forcing their way into the holiday zeitgeist, regardless of quality. "Jingle All the Way" is one of those movies.

Remembered as a comedy that glorifies the hollow commercialism of the holiday season, "Jingle All the Way" was far from a critical darling. But Roger Ebert at least had some praise for it back in 1996, writing:

"I liked a lot of the movie, which is genial and has a lot of energy, but I was sort of depressed by its relentlessly materialistic view of Christmas, and by the choice to go with action and (mild) violence over dialogue and plot. Audiences will like it, I am sure, but I have to raise my hand in reluctant dissent and ask, please, sir, may we have some more goodwill among men? Even TurboMen?"

Honestly, we should probably be throwing more praise at "Jingle All the Way." While it might depict the unfortunate side of holiday shopping greed and consumerism, it's hard to deny how much fun it is to watch Arnold Schwarzenegger scramble to find a Turbo Man action figure, while Sinbad taunts and thwarts him at every turn. It's a cinematic masterpiece compared to "Jingle All the Way 2" with Larry the Cable Guy, proving it's a Christmas movie that didn't need a sequel.

But one of the best parts of "Jingle All the Way" comes from the interaction that Schwarzenegger's Howard Langston has with his deceptively thoughtful, sleazy neighbor Ted (the late, great star of "Saturday Night Live" and "The Simpsons," the one and only Phil Hartman). That's where we get one of the best Christmas movie quotes of all time.

Here are some more memorable quotes from "Jingle All the Way," though they might not be as versatile as our favorite:

"I'm not a pervert! I just was looking for a Turbo Man doll!" – Howard Langston

"How about these stupid letters from kids to Santa at the North Pole: 'Dear Santa, can you send me a bike and a slinky?' No! Your father's been laid off!" – Myron Larabee

"I'm gonna deck your halls, bub." — Huge Santa

"They sit there and use subliminal messages to suck your children's minds out! And I know what I'm talking about because I went to junior college for a semester and I studied psychology so I'm right in there, I know what's going on. And then they sit there and they make your children feel like garbage and you, the father, who's working 24/7 delivering mail so you can make an alimony payment to a woman that slept with everybody at the post office, but me! And then when you get the toy, it breaks and you can't fix it because it's little cheap plastic!" – Myron Larabee

"That really was a bomb? This is a sick world we live in! Sick people!" – Myron Larabee

"You know what? Nobody likes you, Booster." – Myron Larabee

"It's Turbo Time!" – Howard Langston as Turbo Man

"Ta-ta, Turtle Man!" – Myron Larabee as Dementor

#3473. If You Loved 'The Good Daughter,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There are plenty of reasons Peacock’s The Good Daughter is so damn watchable. The performances, for one—Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy are terrific as estranged sisters Sam and Charlotte Quinn. But it’s also a great story, tracing the corrosive effect of a years-ago trauma on the women and their lawyer father (Brendan Gleeson) amid the slow revelation of many extremely dark secrets. If you want more of that flavor of trauma-driven drama with a tight focus on family bonds, there’s one movie you should watch: 2015's Dark Places.

You want buried secrets? Dark Places has seriously buried secrets. Adapted from the Gillian Flynn novel, the film follows Libby Day (Charlize Theron), who survived the mass murder of her family in 1985. The crime is blamed on her brother Ben, a moody loner whose conviction was based in large part on Libby’s own testimony. For a long time, Libby is financially sustained by donations from people who sympathize with her plight, but three decades after the murders, the money has dried up, and Libby is desperate—so desperate, she agrees to help out a “true crime” club that believes her brother is innocent and is working toward his release.

Like The Good Daughter, Dark Places is anchored by a sibling relationship reshaped by the impact of horrifying violence. Libby and Ben’s experience mirrors Sam and Charlie’s in many ways, including in the way both Libby and Ben carry secrets for years after the terrible events that took family from them. The stories are also both compelling mysteries, slowly revealing the shocking truths behind one horrific night, and ultimately allowing the characters to better understand one another.

Dark Places also explores the insular, suffocating nature of small-town life, and how rumor and gossip become a poisonous presence in people’s lives. Libby, Ben, Sam, and Charlie all have to deal with others' assumptions and revelations that they've been betrayed by those closest to them, leading to powerful resolutions. If you loved The Good Daughter, you’ll love this movie. Stream Dark Places on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more stories about family dynamics around secrets, violence, and explosive emotional confrontations? Here are a few more movies fans of The Good Daughter are bound to enjoy.

There’s no violent crime at the heart of this slow-burn drama—just an explosive chaos agent named Kym, played by Anne Hathaway. If your favorite aspect of The Good Daughter was the relationship between sisters Sam and Charlie, then this movie is perfect. Released from rehab to attend her sister’s wedding, Kym is self-hating, angry, and haunted by a terrible event from her childhood. Her sister, Rachel (Rosemary DeWitt), is welcoming, but has never truly forgiven Kym, and the simmering tension between the sisters and the rest of the family drives a drama that you won’t be able to look away from. Stream Rachel Getting Married on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

If you really vibed on the Southern setting, the slow-burn mystery, and the exploration of flawed justice in the modern age depicted in The Good Daughter, check out Where the Crawdads Sing. It’s a slower, dreamier rumination on rural life, violence and its cost, and small-town justice, but it hits the same sweet spot in its story about a woman named Kya (Daisy Edgar-Jones) who was raised in an isolated house in the swamps of North Carolina. Accused in 1969 of a murder, Kya’s story stretches back to her childhood, when she’s slowly abandoned by her entire family, leaving her at age seven to survive on her own. Ostracized as the “swamp girl” by the town, Kya fights to live her life and be loved while facing the unwanted—and violently persistent—attention of the murder victim. It’s about broken families, deeply buried secrets, and what we do to survive. Stream Where the Crawdads Sing on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

The Good Daughter is about life in a small, Southern town, family trauma, and the legal system—which makes A Time to Kill the perfect movie to watch when you finish the show. When a Black man’s daughter is sexually assaulted in Mississippi and her attackers—local members of the Ku Klux Klan—look likely to go free, he violently and publicly murders them. Local lawyer Jake Brigance (Matthew McConaughey) takes on the case, assisted by law student Ellen Roark (Sandra Bullock). They face violent opposition, withering racism, and an unfair legal system that echoes the environment in The Good Daughter in ways fans will appreciate. Stream A Time to Kill on YoutTube or rent it on Prime Video.

The Dry might be as close as you can get to The Good Daughter in terms of tone and story. Although set in Australia instead of the American South, The Dry is a story driven by past crimes and buried secrets in a rural setting just like the show. Twenty years ago, Federal agent Aaron Falk (Eric Bana) fled his hometown when he was suspected of the murder of his girlfriend. When his childhood friend, Luke, appears to have murdered his wife and young son before killing himself, he returns to investigate. The slow revelation of two mysteries—one in the past and one simmering in the drought-stricken present—makes this an ideal companion film to the show. Stream The Dry on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

Set in Boston instead of the South, and focused on male friendships instead of a sisters’ bond, Mystic River nevertheless nails the same atmosphere of dread as The Good Daughter. In 1975, boyhood friends Jimmy, Dave, and Sean are traumatized when Dave is abducted and assaulted by two men. In 1990, the three men remain connected in their Boston neighborhood—Jimmy (Sean Penn) is an ex-convict still connected to local crime, Sean (Kevin Bacon) is a State Police detective, and Dave (Tim Robbins) is a blue-collar worker still haunted by his experience. When Jimmy’s daughter is found murdered and Dave seems implicated, Sean and Jimmy launch investigations from either side of the law, with Dave’s fate hanging in the balance. The ending is powerfully brutal, but this story of secrets and suspicion will resonate with fans of the show. Rent Mystic River on Prime Video.

#3472. Dune Director Admits He’s ‘Deeply Disappointed’ by Showdown With Avengers: Doomsday

The two blockbuster franchises are heading for a massive box-office showdown

Denis Villeneuve isn't thrilled about having to share a release date with Marvel's next Avengers movie. The Dune: Part Three director has admitted he's "deeply disappointed" after Disney scheduled Avengers: Doomsday for the same December release date as his upcoming sci-fi sequel. In an interview with Time, Villeneuve discussed the unusual box-office showdown between the two highly anticipated films, both of which are scheduled to open Dec. 18.

"The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us," Villeneuve told Time, pointing to the challenges surrounding the first two installments. Dune: Part Two was originally expected to arrive in the fall before being pushed to the end of winter because of the Hollywood strikes.

Villeneuve said he had hoped the third movie would finally enjoy a more straightforward theatrical release, without a pandemic or industry shutdown complicating its prospects. Instead, Marvel's biggest franchise is now going head-to-head with his film.

"So I was deeply disappointed," he said. "But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema."

Villeneuve acknowledged that Dune doesn't have the same commercial muscle as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, describing Avengers as a "T. rex" and his franchise as a "sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower." Villeneuve's first two Dune films made $411 million and $715 million at the worldwide box office, while Marvel's Avengers movies have consistently grossed in the billions. "I'm no fool. Those movies are a mammoth," he said, adding that he hopes Dune: Part Three will survive the box-office competition.

Still, the filmmaker isn't necessarily viewing the simultaneous releases as a straightforward rivalry. He suggested the two movies could combine to create one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time. "Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not," Villeneuve told Time. "But I stand proud because I think the film delivers."

Dune: Part Three will adapt elements of Frank Herbert's Dune Messiah, picking up years after the events of Dune: Part Two. Timothée Chalamet returns as Paul Atreides, alongside Zendaya, Florence Pugh, and other familiar faces. Villeneuve has also described the movie as a significant departure from the source material, explaining that the adaptation required substantial creative choices.

Avengers: Doomsday marks the next major ensemble installment in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, with Robert Downey Jr. returning to the franchise in a new role as Doctor Doom. Both films are currently scheduled to hit theaters on Dec. 18, setting up a potentially massive "Dunesday" weekend for movie theaters.

#3471. 21 Best Thanksgiving Movies to Stream This Week

Sandwiched between the kitschy horrors of Halloween and the commercialized merriment of Christmas, Thanksgiving is often unfairly overlooked as a cinematic main course. But while there might not be a feast’s worth of Thanksgiving movies, there is undoubtedly an appetite for Thanksgiving fare in film. Look no further than the inclusion of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Miracle on 34th Street or Wednesday Adams’s sinister (if historically-accurate) re-enactment in Addams Family Values for proof that audiences love turkey’s least favorite holiday. Of course, Thanksgiving tends to get a better treatment on TV, inspiring canonical episodes of Gossip Girl, Friends, Master of None, and, of course, A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving.

Nevertheless, we’ve collected 21 Thanksgiving movies (and Thanksgiving-adjacent movies) that capture the spirit of the holiday—turkey-trotting, tossing the pigskin, carb-loading, fighting with your family, and then overheating in a gorgeous cashmere sweater. Here’s to finding post-meal common ground with one of the titles on this list.

This isn’t known as the quintessential Thanksgiving movie for nothing. You know the story: Steve Martin’s uptight marketing executive, Neal, just wants to travel from New York to Chicago for turkey with his family. His plans for an uneventful trip are foiled again and again by John Candy’s boisterous shower-ring salesman, Del, who’s eager to make friends with Neal during their wayward journey. We will never look at pillows—or rental car agents—the same way again.

Don’t let the word Christmas in the title scare you away. This 2016 ensemble comedy starring Danny Glover, Kimberly Elise, Mo’Nique, and Gabrielle Union has undeniable Thanksgiving vibes. Produced by Will Packer and originally sold to Universal Pictures under the title A Meyers Thanksgiving, Almost Christmas follows the dysfunctional Meyers family as the family patriarch, Walter Meyers (Glover), tries to get through his first holiday season after the death of his wife. While it isn’t exactly about Thanksgiving per se, most of the best moments in Almost Christmas—including Elise chasing Romany Malco away from the table with a shotgun, or the whole table having to pretend to like Mo’Nique’s terrible food—take place during large family gatherings around the dinner table. What could be more Thanksgiving-coded than that?  With an all-star cast of Black actors that also includes J.B. Smoove, Nicole Ari Parker, Omar Epps, and Gladys Knight, Almost Christmas feels like a homecoming full of your favorite uncles and aunties. And, to be fair, isn’t Thanksgiving almost Christmas?

The turkey isn’t the only thing getting carved up in this holiday slasher. Starring Patrick Dempsey and Tik Toker turned recording artist turned film actress Addison Rae, Thanksgiving begins with a Black Friday sale gone horribly awry in Plymouth, Massachusetts, leading to the death of multiple customers. The following year, a murderous slasher wearing a John Carver mask is wreaking havoc in Plymouth, and targeting Rae’s Gaby and her friends. If you’re not feeling warm and gooey on over the holiday, you might want to throw on Thanksgiving and watch Rae and Dempsey’s Sheriff Eric Newton try and track down and escape the clutches of a grisly murderer.

In Jodie Foster’s comedy, Holly Hunter plays Claudia Larson, who returns home for Thanksgiving after losing her job and learning that her daughter (My So-Called Life–era Claire Danes) plans to spend the holiday with a boyfriend. The family she returns to is filled with colorful performances from Anne Bancroft and Charles Durning as her eclectic parents, Robert Downey Jr. as her misanthrope brother, and Dylan McDermott as a semi-mysterious dinner guest.

Fantastic Mr. Fox isn’t technically about Thanksgiving, or even really about humans. And yet, Wes Anderson’s 2009 stop-motion film, featuring the voices of George Clooney and Meryl Streep, has been labeled a Thanksgiving must-watch. Perhaps that’s because the film, based on Roald Dahl’s classic children’s novel, is all about animals trying to escape the tyranny of farmers—something every turkey not lucky enough to be pardoned by the president wishes it could do around Thanksgiving time. Beyond the war between animals and farmers, Anderson’s rustic color palette filled with burnt orange—and the massive feast that brings a diverse array of animals around a dinner table after they successfully joined forces to steal food from their nemeses—are full of the spirit of Thanksgiving.

At times, the titular April’s (Katie Holmes) fate feels as if it rests on whether she’ll successfully cook a turkey in her crowded Lower East Side apartment. As April prepares to host her suburban Pennsylvania family, the high-stakes nature of spending a day hunkered down with relatives—played by Patricia Clarkson, Oliver Platt, Alison Pill, and John Gallagher Jr.—rushes in.

Sometimes getting families together over the holidays is fraught. In this 1997 moody drama directed by Ang Lee, two affluent Connecticut families unravel over Thanksgiving break as their secrets come to lights. The ensemble cast includes stalwart actors Kevin Kline, Joan Allen, Sigourney Weaver as messy parents, and, at that point, up and comers, Tobey Maguire, Elijah Wood, and Christina Ricci as their even more troubled teens. The Ice Storm, which won best screenplay at Cannes Film Festival, is rife with adultery, substance abuse, as well as surprising turns from a host of talented actors and a sharp early film from one of cinema’s most celebrated directors.

Nothing feels more nostalgic during Thanksgiving than watching Snoopy whip up a makeshift meal with jelly beans, popcorn, and mountains of buttered toast for all of his Peanuts pals. And Vince Guraldi’s timeless score makes for a perfect soundtrack to your own festivities.

A Thanksgiving flashback provides key context for the complicated dynamics amongst this group of recently-reunited college friends, played by Glenn Close, Kevin Kline, Jeff Goldblum, Mary Kay Place, and William Hurt. Lawrence Kasdan’s film earned three Oscar nominations, including best picture, original screenplay, and supporting actress for Close.

While not a Thanksgiving-themed film, protagonist Nola Darling (Tracy Camilla Johns) invites all three of her potential suitors to a tense dinner on that very holiday, making her memorable decision between them from her head-of-the-table vantage point. This was most of the world’s introduction to Spike Lee, both as an actor and director, and the electricity is still palpable. And if you’ve gotta have more? You can always stream the 2017 Netflix original series of the same name, starring Lee and DeWanda Wise as Nola Darling.

Rian Johnson’s whodunnit has all the trappings of a Thanksgiving movie, without ever mentioning the holiday. There’s family infighting, Chris Evans in a cable-knit sweater, foggy fall weather, and even a political allegory about the treatment of people of color. Also not about Thanksgiving, but worthy viewing for the full family: Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery, which hit theaters last November.

The same year that Merriam-Webster acknowledged Instagram captions everywhere by adding “Friendsgiving” to the dictionary, a movie of the same name was released. True to its titular tradition, a group of friends convenes for a meal that inevitably devolves into chaos.

While not an outright Thanksgiving movie, 1997’s ensemble dramedy contains some of the most sumptuous shots of food ever committed to film. After the death of their family matriarch, a group of disparate relatives must put aside their differences and reconvene for a weekly Sunday dinner. Starring Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long, Soul Food captures the bonding powers that plates of cornbread, catfish, and collard greens can bring.

This 1976 best picture Oscar winner stars Sylvester Stallone as the eponymous down-on-his-luck boxer, whose fate begins to change with the meeting of his future wife, Adrian (Talia Shire). “To you, it’s Thanksgiving. To me, it’s Thursday,” Rocky tells Adrian as he whisks her away from a disastrous family feast minutes after her brother Paulie (Burt Young) hurls her turkey into the nearby alley. As fans of the franchise, which has debuted several films over the Thanksgiving holiday, know, their Thanksgiving meet-cute will stand the test of time.

Thanksgiving isn’t always about bickering with your blood relatives. Spend Thanksgiving with Instant Family, which stars Mark Wahlberg and Rose Byrne as Pete and Ellie Wagner, an unwitting couple who, overnight, become parents to three foster children. Their decision to become parents happens over  a tense Thanksgiving dinner where Ellie’s family shares they don’t think that Pete and Ellie were ever really cut out to be parents. In an effort to prove them wrong, the Wagners wind up biting off more than they bargained for as they become foster parents to three children, the eldest played by Madame Web star Isabela Merced.

Before Greta Gerwig forced Noah Baumbach to write Barbie with her, there was Mistress America. Written by the real-life couple who helmed the billion dollar blockbuster, this 2015 Sundance favorite centers on the unlikely friendship between Lola Kirke’s Tracy, a first-year college student alone in New York, and Gerwig’s Brooke, the Times Square-living twentysomething who will soon become her stepsister. Conflict between the pair gets resolved on Thanksgiving at New York City’s Veselka, a Ukrainian institution where pierogis stand in for the traditional bird.

Greta Gerwig must really love Thanksgiving. The auteur’s Oscar-nominated take on the Louisa May Alcott classic is brimming with cozy, Thanksgiving-esque vibes. Set largely in the weeks before Christmas, the March sisters (Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Eliza Scanlen, and Florence Pugh) and matriarch (Laura Dern) battle wits, trot through the snow, and stage living room plays in a film that feels reminiscent of many a-family gatherings.

“First, let’s give thanks to our families not being here. It’s always easier without the family,” Adam Sandler’s George Simmons, a stand-up comedian who has been newly diagnosed with cancer, says to a group of new friends. In Judd Apatow’s 2009 dramedy, George attempts to revamp his fledgling career in the eleventh hour with the help of aspiring comic Ira Wright (Seth Rogen). At one point, he  joins the younger talent’s friendsgiving festivities, where the table is surrounded by stars including Jonah Hill, Jason Schwartzman, Aubrey Plaza, and Bo Burnham.

In one of the newer entries to the turkey day canon, Stephen Karam adapts his 2015 Pulitzer finalist play of the same name, exploring the long-held resentments and deeply-rooted admiration that live in an East Coast family. Jayne Houdyshell reprises her Tony-winning role as Deirdre alongside a stacked ensemble, including Richard Jenkins, June Squibb, Beanie Feldstein, Steven Yeun, and Amy Schumer, all gathered in a drab Chinatown apartment for Thanksgiving.

Prisoners finds Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal teaming up to find a pair of missing girls who were abducted after Thanksgiving dinner in Conyers, Pennsylvania. EGOT recipient Viola Davis also stars in the thriller as the mother of one of the kidnapped girls. Directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve, Prisoners is an unconventional and unsettling Thanksgiving film.

Another unconventional choice, Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man is arguably the only superhero movie that doubles as a Thanksgiving movie. While the central action follows Tobey Maguire’s Peter Parker, there’s a pivotal scene set at Thanksgiving dinner that directly follows a heated battle between Spider-Man and the Green Goblin (a.k.a Norman Osborne, played by Willem Dafoe.) Parker and Osborne have Thanksgiving dinner together with MJ (Kirsten Dunst), Harry Osborne (James Franco), and Aunt May (Rosemary Harris). During the meal, Osborne comes to the stunning realization that Peter Parker is, in fact, Spider-Man. Others have already made the case that the first Spider-Man film deserves to be included in the Thanksgiving canon. The way Dafoe carves the turkey is also both sinister and iconic, as is Maguire apologizing for his tardiness because he “had to beat an old lady with a stick to get these cranberries.”

#3468. I Tried Coros' New 'Expedition-Focused' Smartwatch, and I'm Impressed

Coros has unveiled the Vertix 4, an “expedition-focused” update to the Vertix 2 and 2S. Coros says it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

This watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

That price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is currently on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that launched earlier this year.

Built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

Previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

Coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:

Music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

On paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.

It’s undeniably adorable to watch the Olaf animatronic walking itself around the Kingdom of Arendelle at Disneyland Paris. But one of the biggest drawbacks that has come with introducing a “living” animatronic Olaf to guests in Disney’s European theme park is the fact that sometimes it malfunctions, which can be shocking to witness.

The incidents of Olaf failing, freezing, and falling over are adding up, most recently happening during a holiday performance of the Arendelle Carolers. It’s a frightening sight when it happens, though Josh Gad has kept a sense of humor about it all, as the actor who is responsible for the snowman's lovable personality. However, with this latest incident, it actually brought me joy to see that Cast Members seemed to have a plan for helping get Olaf removed from the stage without traumatizing guests too deeply. Check out the Instagram clip below to see exactly what happened:

A post shared by Marissa Huston | Mom of 4 | Europe Travel (@4kidsandapassport)

This major snowman emergency occurred in World of Frozen during a live performance. Olaf was animated and walking around the stage like the adorable snowman he is until he suddenly fell over, which I’m sure led to audible gasps from the gathered crowd. Stopping the show, the carolers lined up in their purple coats and scarves, essentially creating a wall to allow Cast Members to gather the beloved character and remove him. All the while, they smiled and waved, presumably in the hopes of not upsetting the children.

I almost feel bad about having a laugh about it all, but the whole incident is oddly amusing to watch. And with the growing number of malfunctions that have happened since introducing the animatronic figure, it’s hard not to be delighted by the absurdity of it all.

Only a couple of weeks before this memorable moment, Olaf closed his eyes and froze while mid-dance before ultimately defrosting and continuing with the show. So, I’m not surprised to see that the Arendelle Carolers seem to have a plan for whisking the happy-go-lucky snowman away as quickly as possible.

Getting to meet beloved Disney characters is a longtime tradition, where animated characters become live-action characters in the parks. While we knew that Disney Parks had been working on robots for a few years, it’s been really incredible to see the snowman walking, singing, and moving to the beat.

Olaf even received his own sleigh to help transport him to the stage at the foot of North Mountain for this sweet 15-minute family show. But that has not stopped the glitches or the full-blown shutdowns, instead giving us even more moments of malfunction. As much joy as all of this has brought me, I do hope that there will come a day when all of this gets smoothed out, if for no other reason than to not have to force parents to explain to their children what’s going on.

While more Frozen films are in the works, we won’t see Frozen 3 until November 24, 2027. Until then, I’m hoping we’ll get more Olaf fun in and around the Disney theme parks.

#3466. What Makes Blade Runner 2099's Mercerism Subplot So Relevant [Exclusive]

More spoilery than spoilers. This article contains, you guessed it, spoilers for "Blade Runner 2099."

After two movies, several short films, the anime show "Black Lotus," and numerous novels and comics, how many directions are left to take the "Blade Runner" franchise? Well, that's easy. You simply go back to the original source material. "Blade Runner 2099" creator and showrunner Silka Luisa embraced the tall task of picking up the classic story where previous media left off — by going straight to the book that inspired it all.

Those who've read Philip K. Dick's "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" will recognize the author's fingerprints all over the Mercerism plotline that rises to the fore late in "Blade Runner 2099." In the novel, this idiosyncratic religion centers on Wilber Mercer, a holy figure who climbs a mountain on a pilgrimage. The catch is, he does so while having rocks thrown at him mercilessly, inspiring the idea to recreate his torturous ascent through a virtual reality device known as an empathy box. This was one of the biggest aspects that both "Blade Runner" movies completely skipped, preferring to focus on the more grounded details of this cyberpunk world while eschewing the spiritual.

That finally changes here, as I discussed with Luisa during a press junket. "I was always fascinated by Mercerism," she explained. "Just the idea that there was a religion that was technology-based where people would be completely isolated, but then join through technology so that they could feel empathy with each other — that feels so current." She went on to theorize:

"If you sold [empathy boxes] today, I genuinely think people would buy them. There is this deep longing for connection, and we no longer know how to get in a room and be with each other."

Given the digital horrors we've normalized on an everyday basis in recent years (the impending threat of a superintelligence bent on our destruction, generative AI, and the ever-present hellscape that is social media), it's not too much of a leap to take "Blade Runner 2099" creator Silka Luisa at her word about Mercerism. Somewhere, there almost certainly would be a segment of the population all too happy to strap themselves into an empathy box device and electroshock themselves into feeling the same pain that Wilber Mercer supposedly did. (Of course, his entire ascent is eventually revealed to be a staged incident that never actually happened, but that's neither here nor there.)

But, even more than that unsettling hypothetical, Luisa had an even better reason to introduce the concept of Mercerism into "2099." As she excitedly told me:

"[...] Just from a creative and an imagination standpoint, it was so exciting to be like, 'Okay, I only have a couple words of description here, but what does an empathy box look like? How do we find references from the real-world that we can build out into it?'"

In the series, Michelle Yeoh's Replicant Olwen gets an up close and personal experience with an unfriendly Mercerite cultist. For Luisa, this provided a unique opportunity to flesh out what was in the scripts:

"Trying to design the murals that are in the chapel, all the little paraphernalia that would go with it, who would be practitioners of it. That's just such fun world-building that, I mean, what other show are you gonna get to do that on?"

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" (you can read our review here) are now streaming on Prime Video.
