#3449. The Home Depot Is Giving Away Free Milwaukee, DeWalt, and Makita Cordless Power Tools for Black Friday

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

As anyone who has ever shopped at The Home Depot (or any hardware store) knows, power tools are expensive. That’s why Black Friday at The Home Depot is so important: It’s the perfect opportunity to get the tools you’ve been wanting at some pretty steep discounts. And the best deals even give you a free tool if you purchase a starter kit from one of the major tool brands (Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee).

Here’s how this year's “buy one, get one” (BOGO) deal works: Pick out a starter kit from one of the brands, add it to your cart, and you’ll be presented with a list of available tools you can add (they’ll be marked “FREE,” so you can’t get confused). When you go to check out, the price of the tool will be listed as “SAVINGS.”

Here are the starter kits you can choose from:

Ryobi ONE+ 18V Starter Kit (includes one 4.0Ah and one 2.0Ah battery and charger). Cost: $99.

DeWalt 20V Max Starter Kit (includes 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah batteries and charger). Cost: $199.

Makita 18V LXT Starter Pack (includes two 5.0Ah batteries and a rapid charger). Cost: $199.

Milwaukee M18 FUEL Combo Kit (includes a brushless, cordless hammer drill and an impact driver). Cost: $399.

Note that the Ryobi, DeWalt, and Milwaukee offers include 14 free tools to choose from, while the Makita offer only includes 8. Also, note that while the Ryobi starter kit is your cheapest option for a free tool, the batteries included are weaker. The DeWalt or Makita batteries cost more, but offer more power and flexibility.

Some of the deals go beyond just getting a freebie. For example, if you choose the DeWalt Starter Kit for $199, you can get an Atomic 20V Max impact wrench that normally costs $239 for free, which is a significant savings even if you already have batteries and a charger and don’t really need those items (plus, you can never have too many batteries).

The Home Depot is also offering deep discounts on just about everything in the store. Some of the most notable tool deals include:

50% off this DeWalt Cordless Brushless Oscillating Multi Tool, including battery and charger

33% off this Ryobi Combo Kit, an incredible deal for a circular saw, reciprocating saw, and a power drill/driver plus two batteries and a charger; the batteries are small, but this is a great deal on a starter kit.

42% off this Combo Kit from Milwaukee, including a Packout toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger—a massive deal for anyone who needs to tool up rapidly.

45% off this Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit from Ryobi, which includes a battery and charger.

That only scratches the surface—if you’ve ever needed anything from Home Depot, Black Friday is the day to run out and get it.

Of course, Black Friday can be a little chaotic, so here are a few tips to maximize your savings and experience:

Check online and in-store. Some deals are in-store only, and some items (especially BOGO tools) may not be available at your nearest location—make sure you enter your ZIP code when you’re checking out to ensure you won’t have any problems.

Consider whether you need more batteries and chargers. Depending on your existing collection of batteries and chargers, buying more to get the discount may or may not make sense.

There's no price matching or rain checks. Remember that the store won’t honor price-matching or offer rain checks on Black Friday items.

Cyber Monday will have deals, too. More deals will be rolled out on Cyber Monday (November 30), which may include items you want but don’t see on sale for Black Friday. But keep in mind that Black Friday prices probably won’t go any lower—so snap up what you need as soon as you can.

Sign up for text alerts to save a little more. Home Depot offers a $5 coupon (off a purchase of $50 or more) when you sign up for email or text alerts, which you may be able to apply to your Black Friday purchase for a little extra savings.

Home Depot isn’t the only store offering free tool giveaways:

Like Home Depot, Lowes is offering BOGO tools with the purchase of starter kits from major tool brands.

Tractor Supply Co. has a wide range of BOGO tool offers during its Black Friday Event.

If you’re looking for outdoor equipment, note that Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s aren’t offering a BOGO deal this year, but the first 250 customers at each physical store will receive a free “mystery promo card” valued between $10 and $500. If you’re going to go for this, plan to line up early—250 cards are going to go fast.

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools..

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

#3448. The 6 Most Bingeable Crime Shows You Can Finish In a Weekend

Sometimes we seek out something with a darker tone and narrative as a means of escape. It’s why crime shows continue to be a go-to genre for television fans. The genre offers viewers a chance to dive into a gritty underworld and watch crime unfold before their eyes. Whether it be a murder mystery of a syndicate of unsavory individuals, the stories crime shows get to tell keep us glued to our screens. If you’re seeking out a crime drama and only have a single weekend to watch, we’ve got six shows perfect for you!

From award-winning masterpieces to ripped-from-the-headlines dramatizations, the six crime shows on this list offer a brilliant hook and a satisfying conclusion. Though there are countless long-running crime shows that are equally as good, you simply won’t be able to complete them in the hours allotted. These six you certainly can! Once you start, you simply won’t be able to stop until the final credits roll.

No crime thriller has captured our attention quite like the critically acclaimed Adolescence. Created by Jack Thorne and Stephen Graham, and directed by Philip Barantini, the four-part crime story follows 13-year-old Jamie Miller (Owen Cooper), who is arrested in a pre-dawn raid for the fatal stabbing of a female classmate. Filmed entirely in single, continuous takes, the series follows Jamie’s devastated family, a lead detective, and a clinical psychologist as they piece together what drove an seemingly ordinary boy to commit murder. Along the way, the story examines the real-world fallout of cyberbullying, social media pressure, and online "manosphere" radicalization on young men. Adolescence refuses to rely on sensationalized twists, opting instead to build natural real-time tension.

Each hour-long episode captures a single moment of the harrowing ordeal. By filming in a singular unbroken shot, the approach keeps the tension immediate and pulls viewers directly into the room during police procedures, interviews, and family confrontations. The narrative tackles modern themes through a mesmerizing, fresh lens that captures a wider chain of social and family pressures. The story stays concentrated on the immediate aftermath and psychological toll rather than stretching out a slow investigation. Adolescence is an acting showcase. Cooper’s breakout debut is sensational. It’s a raw, natural performance that deserved the massive award sweep. Graham as his father, Eddie, and Erin Doherty as Briony Ariston, the psychologist evaluating him, deliver stellar turns. Adolescence became a gamechanger in miniseries storytelling, reshaping how short-form narratives can be told.

The greatest multi-season crime drama of all time is Broadchurch. Created by Chris Chibnall, the three-season drama follows Detective Inspector Alec Hardy (David Tennant) and Detective Sergeant Ellie Miller (Olivia Colman) as they investigate major crimes in a close-knit English coastal town. The first two seasons focus on the murder of 11-year-old Danny Latimer (Oskar McNamara) and its legal fallout, while the third season centers on the investigation of Trish Winterman’s (Julie Hesmondhalgh) sexual assault. Throughout the series, intense police inquiries and media scrutiny expose hidden secrets that fracture the tight-knit community. A standout series with a brilliant acting ensemble, Broadchurch pairs a gripping mystery with grounded, character-driven drama and raw emotional fallout. From the very first episode, Broadchurch hooks you. The crime is established, the town is reeling, and the individuals investigating the shocking murder have engaging character flaws that may prevent them from doing their job at the best of their ability.

Broadchurch shows how a single crime shatters a tight-knit coastal community and reshapes everyday relationships over time. The series lingers on grief, paranoia, media scrutiny, and long-term consequences. Its grounded approach treats tragedy as something that permanently alters people. Filming on location in places like West Bay, Dorset, gives the show a moody coastal atmosphere where familiar neighbors suddenly look like strangers. Chibnall keeps viewers guessing with slow-burn suspense and a steady stream of suspicious leads rather than relying on obvious tropes. Led by Colman and Tennant, who have impeccable chemistry, the ensemble features a murderer’s row of UK stars including Jodie Whittaker, Jonathan Bailey, David Bradley, Alfred Enoch, Arthur Darvill, Jacob Anderson, Marianne Jean-Baptiste, Phoebe Waller-Bridge, James D’Arcy, Eve Myles, Shaun Dooley, and Lenny Henry. With three seasons of eight tight episodes, Broadchurch is absolutely a show you can achieve in a weekend because it’s addictive. Each episode introduces new clues, red herrings, and emotional cliffhangers that naturally compel you to hit "next episode."

One of the best self-contained American crime dramas of the decade is the brilliant Mare of Easttown. Written by Brad Ingelsby and directed by Craig Zobel, the seven-episode series tells the story of Mare Sheehan (Kate Winslet), a small-town Pennsylvania detective. While investigating the murder of a local teenage mother and reopening a year-old missing person's case, Mare struggles to keep her personal life from unraveling. As she uncovers dark secrets within her tight-knit community, she is also forced to confront her own deep-seated grief and family struggles. Mare of Easttown pairs a gripping small-town murder investigation with a deeply lived-in community where every individual is raw, authentic, and grappling with a broken reality.

Mare of Easttown is a masterpiece in storytelling. Ingelsby crafts a fictionalized version of Pennsylvania's Delaware County that feels immersive. The show grounds its mystery in local rhythms, community loyalty, addiction, and a carefully coached regional dialect. Across seven episodes, the show builds from a slow-burn setup into a twist-heavy final stretch that keeps you thoroughly engaged. And yet, beyond the investigation is a beautiful character-centric story. Winslet brings emotional exhaustion, rough edges, and quiet vulnerability to a woman navigating grief, family strain, and town expectations. Mare of Easttown features a stellar cast that elevates the narrative. With a supporting ensemble featuring Julianne Nicholson, Jean Smart, Evan Peters, and Guy Pearce, Mare of Easttown is built around the town's weighted, tangled relationships. Mare of Easttown is a show you’ll wish had a second season because it’s exceptionally executed.

HBO is a breeding ground for top-notch crime dramas. In 2016, The Night Of was proof as to why the premium cable network maintains a strong grip on sensational storytelling. Written by Richard Price and Steven Zaillian, and based on the original Criminal Justice plot by Peter Moffat, the eight-episode crime thriller follows Nasir "Naz" Khan (Riz Ahmed), a mild-mannered Pakistani-American college student in New York City who wakes up from a night of drinking and drugs to find the young woman he met stabbed to death. With no memory of what happened, Naz flees in panic, only to be quickly arrested and charged with her murder after police find the suspected weapon in his pocket. As streetwise defense attorney John Stone (John Turturro) takes on his case, the series examines the flaws of the American criminal justice system and how awaiting trial at Rikers Island transforms Naz. A truly remarkable story, The Night Of treats a murder accusation as a gateway into character psychology and institutional reality.

The Night Of prioritizes character over twist. The story tracks how a single night's events reshape Naz, his defense attorneys, his family, and the investigators. By examining courtroom friction, Rikers Island survival, institutional negligence, and cultural bias, the series is grounded with authenticity. From its Kafkaesque opening night to its cinematography and sound design, the pacing builds dread and immersion. The practical New York set pieces became a character of their own. Ahmed and Turturro are brilliant. Ahmed’s Emmy-winning turn is built on raw emotion, making him an underdog that you desperately wish to see earn justice. In a career-best turn, Turturro embodies Stone, down to his eczema-plagued exterior. Joined by strong performances from Michael K. Williams and Billy Camp, the series is a strong showing of realistic characters. Only eight strong episodes are needed to tell a complete, buttressing story. The story moves from a police procedural and murder mystery to a courtroom drama with seamless ease.

Perhaps we have to thank Christopher Nolan for allowing superhero films and series to move beyond the generic booms and pows. Spun off from Matt Reeves’ feature film The Batman, The Penguin drops the titular character into a bona fide criminal underworld that just so happens to have iconic IP. Created by Lauren LeFranc, The Penguin follows mid-level mobster Oswald "Oz" Cobb (Colin Farrell) as he attempts to seize control of Gotham City's criminal underworld. Following the death of crime boss Carmine Falcone (Mark Strong) and the catastrophic flooding of the city, Oz exploits the resulting power vacuum to push a new drug trade and dismantle rival factions from within. Along the way, he forms a fragile mentorship with a young street kid, Victor Aguilar (Rhenzy Feliz), while navigating a brutal turf war against Carmine's ruthless daughter, Sofia Falcone (Cristin Milioti), and the Maroni crime family. The Penguin prioritizes grounded mob storytelling, character psychology, and high-stakes power struggles over superhero spectacle for a fully-realized masterpiece.

Four criminal masterminds. One of them was always going to be yours. Here is who comes for you, why they picked you out of everyone available, and what they want from the encounter.

Your nemesis does not want to beat you. He wants to know you completely, and he is patient enough to wait for it. The frightening part is how good the conversation is.

Your nemesis is not after money, territory or revenge. He is after a demonstration, and you are the person he has chosen to prove his point on.

Your nemesis respects you, which sounds flattering until you work out what it means. He chose you because nobody else was worth his time.

Your nemesis has no personal interest in you whatsoever, and that is precisely what makes him unsurvivable. You are not a rival. You are a stop on the way.

Following the flooding of Gotham City and Carmine Falcone's death, the eight-episode HBO miniseries plays like a gritty crime drama in the vein of The Sopranos and classic mafia cinema. Rather than softening Oz into a neat anti-hero, showrunner LeFranc examines how manipulation, betrayal, and his fraught relationship with his mother, Francis Cobb (Deirdre O’Connell), shape a genuinely monstrous rise to power. Farrell delivers a transformative turn as the iconic character, balancing dark humor and calculated ruthlessness. Opposite him, Milioti brings a sensational spin on a woman with intense vulnerability. She finds a balance of menace and psychological chaos while still holding her rival’s feet to the fire. O’Connell is the ensemble's unsung hero, bringing fragile despair to a woman slowly losing control. Her ability to maintain quiet fury, manipulation, and heavy secrets tied to Oz's past makes her a brilliantly complex character. And then Feliz will absolutely break your heart, with his demise being the hardest moment of the entire series. The Penguin moves at a perfectly brisk pace, with Gotham's underworld playing like a gritty crime drama that goes beyond a traditional comic book adaptation. The Penguin is so good, you’ll keep begging for more. ​​​​​​​

Chances are you are familiar with The Staircase thanks to the infamous true-crime docuseries by Jean-Xavier de Lestrade. In 2022, the story of the documentary and its subject was dramatized in utterly brilliant fashion. Created by Antonio Campos, The Staircase centers on crime novelist Michael Peterson (Colin Firth), who becomes the prime suspect in his wife Kathleen’s (Toni Collette) murder after she is found dead at the bottom of a staircase in their North Carolina home in 2001. The eight-episode series chronicles the resulting 16-year legal battle and how deep-seated family secrets and shifting allegiances tear the Petersons' blended family apart. It also weaves in the behind-the-scenes story of the French documentary crew filming the defense, exploring how competing theories and true-crime storytelling shape the truth. The Staircase moves beyond the headlines, uniting high-caliber acting with a shifting, non-prescriptive structure that explores competing theories around Kathleen’s death rather than handing down a simple verdict.

Spanning timelines from 2001 to 2017, the eight-episode series examines the shocking saga through ambiguity and shifting perspectives. Incorporating the arrival of a French documentary crew filming the defense adds a layer to how true crime is constructed and manipulated. And let’s just say the actual individuals were none too pleased with some artistic liberties. That said, it’s a fascinating take that benefits those familiar with the documentary. Firth and Collette bring their exquisite dramatic skills to anchor a sensational ensemble where the taint runs deep. That includes Michael Stuhlbarg, Juliette Binoche, Rosemarie DeWitt, Patrick Schwarzenegger, Dane DeHaan, and Parker Posey. The compact crime thriller plays as a high-stakes family drama that zeroes in on how secrets, shifting trust, and a 16-year legal battle can destroy any semblance of normalcy. It's a perfect weekend watch.

Those hopes have now been squashed by HBO's boss.

Casey Bloys, chairman and CEO of HBO and Max content, shared several updates on upcoming projects with Deadline in September, following a successful night at the Emmys for the company. That included The Last of Us, with Bloys saying that, "Craig [Mazin] has planned it as the final season."

Mazin is the co-creator and showrunner of the series. After The Last of Us, he's moving on to create a Dungeons & Dragons show, a sequel to Baldur's Gate 3, for HBO.

After adapting the first game in the first season of the show, HBO split The Last of Us Part 2 across two seasons to reflect the game's dual protagonists. Season 2 tells the story of Ellie's (Bella Ramsey) quest for revenge following the death of Joel (Pedro Pascal) and her hunt for Abby (Kaitlyn Dever). Season 3 will flip the perspective, retelling the same period of time as season 2 from Abby's point of view. This will also introduce the character of Lev, played by Michelle Mao.

Neil Druckmann, co-creator of the game series, co-created the HBO show alongside Mazin. Druckmann served as a showrunner and writer for the first two seasons but stepped away from work on season 3. Recently he has continued to distance himself and Naughty Dog from the show, especially after the response to the second season was less than stellar. In a recent interview with The Washington Post, he affirmed that Naughty Dog had no creative role in the final season before teasing that he still has plans for the future of the franchise.

As for when season 3 of the show will actually be released, Bloys reiterated that it is scheduled for 2027. He didn't give further details on a specific date or window beyond that. Don't worry though, as Sony is currently working on a God of War series for Prime Video starring Dave Bautista. The hunger for more game adaptations will be sated.

#3445. PS5s Are in Short Supply for Black Friday, but You Can Still Buy One

There may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a new, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

If you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

There are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a new console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. They're generally more expensive than the original price and more expensive than refurbished units as well. Here are some examples:

Best Buy lists this PS5 Pro with PlayStation Portal Remote for $2,134.99.

GameStop lists a Ghost of Yotei Gold Limited Edition PS5 bundle for $769.99 ($731.49 for GameStop Pros).

Best Buy lists a PS5 Slim with an external drive for $979.99.

By far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. The average price of used PS5 consoles here is hovering between $300 and $500, which seems fairly reasonable. But with Facebook Marketplace, the number of potential red flags rises with the demand for the product.

I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3442. What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

One of the great things about going to the movies by yourself is that, technically speaking, you’re not alone. Even if you’re the only person in the auditorium, somebody thought about what you might like to watch, put it on the calendar, and made sure there was a place for you to sit.

That’s something worth being grateful for this Thanksgiving.

Earlier this month, IndieWire surveyed the programming at independent movie theaters across the United States on Election Night. Continuing that exercise over Thanksgiving weekend reveals another delightful cross-section of American film culture — albeit with considerably more cannibalism. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

At the Music Box Theatre in Chicago, where audiences have spent more than two decades celebrating Thanksgiving by singing along to “The Sound of Music,” moviegoers can also catch Ruggero Deodato’s “Cannibal Holocaust” late Friday night. It’s hard to imagine the Von Trapps sticking around for that one, but there’s something lovely about a neighborhood institution accommodating both crowds.

In Seattle, the Beacon is observing its own Thanksgiving tradition with “Blood Rage,” the gloriously ridiculous slasher that made cranberry sauce an enduring point of reference for a certain subset of horror fans. For a somewhat more realistic depiction of the horrors of going home for Thanksgiving, SALA Event Center in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is showing Jodie Foster’s “Home for the Holidays.”

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Brattle Theatre is celebrating Black Friday with a double feature of “Chopping Mall” and “Night of the Comet.” If you’d rather watch people die in a shopping mall than go to one yourself, that’s certainly an economical alternative. Meanwhile, Minneapolis’ Trylon Cinema is spending the biggest shopping weekend of the year celebrating the work of documentary filmmaker Barbara Kopple, screening her Oscar-winning “Harlan County, U.S.A.” and “American Dream” as part of a series dedicated to class struggle.

Thanksgiving also marks the 50th anniversary of the Band’s legendary farewell concert, held at San Francisco’s Winterland Ballroom in 1976. At Film Streams in Omaha, Nebraska, audiences can spend Friday morning watching Martin Scorsese’s “The Last Waltz.” That half a century later, people are still getting together to experience a concert most of them weren’t alive to attend speaks to one of the more miraculous things movies can do.

And in Portland, Oregon, stop-motion animation studio LAIKA is expressing its gratitude to its hometown audience by offering free screenings of “Wildwood“ on Sunday at theaters across the area, including the historic Hollywood Theatre. Considering how many thousands of hours of human labor go into making a stop-motion animated feature, there’s something especially sweet about giving people whose real home served as the setting a chance to enjoy the outcome together.

Of course, what Americans celebrate on Thanksgiving — and whether they celebrate it at all — varies considerably. On Wednesday, California Indian Nations College is presenting a free screening of “People of the West,” a documentary series examining the history of California’s Indigenous peoples from Indigenous perspectives, in Palm Desert. At the historic Raymond Theatre in Raymond, Washington, a free Saturday screening of a documentary about the Qwayat Canoe Society’s journey to Nisqually offers an opportunity to learn more about a living Indigenous tradition.

And for anyone navigating a particularly painful holiday season, a film festival in Magnolia, Texas, is making a different kind of space. Presented by the nonprofit My Grief Angels, Grief Fest is hosting an in-person community screening on Black Friday, with films also available to watch virtually throughout Thanksgiving weekend. Dedicated to exploring loss and healing through cinema, the festival recognizes just how complicated an invitation to celebrate can be.

There are innumerable ways to spend a long weekend like this, and movies aren’t a substitute for the people we wish we could spend it with. But the wonderful thing about indie exhibition is just how much of it depends on random people thinking about other random people. Someone has to remember that a certain movie exists. Then someone else has to think it might mean something to you. And finally a different person has to care enough to bring it all together.

Whether you’re somebody who spends every Thanksgiving with the same people or a cinephile whose traditions are still taking shape, consider making a little time for your local movie theater this weekend. Thank the person who takes your ticket, and tell the programmer when you love something they booked. Maybe even invite that friend you’ve been meaning to catch up with.

There are so many extraordinary works of art to see in this lifetime and never quite enough time to see them all. How lucky we are to get to watch some of them together.

#3441. 63 Years Later, CBS's Legendary 70-Episode Series Still Has the Only Vampire Worth Watching

Check out the 5 best Grandpa-centric episodes of the classic sitcom

It’s Fangsgiving here at Polygon, our Thanksgiving celebration of stories about fanged creatures of all types and especially vampires. I didn't want to be left out, but, to be honest, I always thought vampires were kind of dumb. They're a horror movie staple, but they’re rarely all that scary. There’s usually a romantic element to their stories that I also find tiresome. Perhaps I’ve just never seen the right vampire movies, but overall I find vampires to be pretty lame.

The only vampire character I ever really had any affection for is Grandpa Munster from the 1964 black-and-white sitcom The Munsters.

The Munsters debuted in 1964 and lasted for just two seasons, but in that time they produced a whopping 70 episodes. The show is about a family of monsters living a normal life in the suburbs and freaking out nearly everyone they encounter. The head of the family is Herman Munster (Fred Gwynne), who is Frankenstein’s monster. He is married to a vampire named Lily (Yvonne De Carlo), and they have​​​​​​​ a werewolf son named Eddie (Butch Patrick). Also living with them is their entirely normal, non-monster niece, Marilyn (Beverley Owen/Pat Priest). And best of all is Grandpa Munster, a several-hundred-year-old vampire​​​​​​​ played by Al Lewis.

While Lily, Eddie and Marilyn were amusing characters in their own right, the best episodes and moments of the show focus on Herman and Grandpa — especially when the two are at odds, which is often. Herman is a dim-witted, affable, optimistic monster, but he can get a bit petulant and baby-like when he doesn’t get his way. Grandpa, meanwhile, is a scheming inventor who often toils away in the family basement, which serves as his laboratory​​​​​​​, which is a frequent source of funny stories on the show. He's very smart, very sarcastic, but also emotional. He’ll quickly become jealous of not being included in something or will overreact to small slights. Also, because he’s hundreds of years old, a recurring gag has Grandpa talking about knowing long-dead historical figures like Genghis Khan and Jack the Ripper.​​​​​​​

To be clear, Grandpa is a pretty crappy vampire. A running gag on the show is his trying (and failing) to bite people. He also can go out during the day and casts a reflection without issue. So, really, he’s a vampire in name only, which might scare off some vampire purists. But if you’re interested in checking out some great Grandpa-centric episodes of The Munsters, here are five of the best.

Another running joke in The Munsters is that Grandpa has been married many, many times — 167, according to one episode — but when a woman from Sioux City, Iowa, claims​​​​​​​ that Grandpa is her lost husband, he’s certain that she isn’t. That is, until Grandpa finds out the woman is incredibly rich. Suddenly, Grandpa is sure this is his wife and decides to move in with her.

Grandpa is feeling lonelier than usual, which prompts him to call the services of a matrimonial agency he finds in the newspaper. Grandpa then turns all of his eccentric charms on a seemingly normal woman​​​​​​​, all of which should scare her off, but they don’t. In time, we find out she’s a black widow scheming to marry Grandpa and then kill him off.

Eddie wants to bring a pet to school for the pet fair, but the family’s pet dragon “Spot” and pet bat “Igor” refuse to go. So Grandpa turns himself into a bat and pretends to be Igor and lets Eddie take him to school​​​​​​​. Unfortunately, Eddie and a friend with a pet squirrel decide to trade pets for the weekend. If that weren’t bad enough, Eddie’s friend’s dad is an astronaut who plans to shoot the bat into space.

After Herman wrecks the Munster Koach in a race, Grandpa builds the Drag-u-la, a race car built off a coffin body. This episode is especially good because it focuses squarely on the hilarious Grandpa/Herman relationship, complete with conflict and some camaraderie​​​​​​​, as the two end up scheming to win together.

Another great Grandpa/Herman episode features the two making a normal trip to the bank​​​​​​​, where they are mistaken for a pair of robbers wearing Halloween masks. They are quickly given all the money in the vault and then must figure out how to return it without looking like they are crooks returning to the scene of the crime.

With Ae's plan to transform Nong Khal Temple into a massive temple redevelopment, the trio takes part in a whole new “Mega Merit Project,” one that involves even more money, power and, of course, crime. "These two worlds – religion and politics – share the same instruments of power used to sway people’s hearts,” Wongwan explained.

With both seasons streaming on Netflix, this underrated, fast-paced drama makes for an easy binge. With Thai society and religion at the forefront, the series, which made history as the first Southeast Asian Netflix Original series to be renewed for a second season, offers a unique glimpse into the dark secrets of religion and politics, while still being entertaining and nail-biting for viewers. Both mowers are designed to remove much of the manual work associated with yard maintenance. Once configured, these mowers can manage multiple mowing zones, customize schedules, and varied cutting heights.

Priced at $1,599, the LUBA mini 2 is a fairly substantial investment, but the $400 Black Friday discount and free wash stand make it a bit easier to justify. Similarly, the LUBA 3 gets a more significant $800 savings, plus the wash stand. If you’ve been considering a robotic lawn mower to bring some automation to the outdoors, these Black Friday offers are worth a look.

#3438. Dungeon Crawler Carl: Allies & Enemies Will Officially Keep You Busy Until Book 9

One of the big breakout surprise hits of the 202s is definitely Dungeon Crawler Carl. While Matt Dinniman's fantasy series started life as a self-published affair in 2019, it was picked up by Amazon and really started to blow up in 2024. Now, in 2026, Dungeon Crawler Carl is even bigger than ever. And while the next book in the series is, if you can believe it, the ninth in less than a decade, I'd say the fun is only just beginning.

It's not too hard to see why Dungeon Crawler Carl is as big as it is. Dinniman's adventures feel like a traditional role-playing game come to life, set in a world story where Earth has been destroyed by aliens and human survivors are forced into an 18-level underground labyrinth to compete in an intergalactic reality television show. It's Hunger Games meets Dungeons & Dragons, so it should come as little surprise that the world translates as well as it does into an actual RPG. From a Lit-RPG to a literal RPG, in other words.

As you may know by now, Renegade Game Studios has developed a full-blooded tabletop adaptation based on the world and characters of Dungeon Crawler Carl. One person acts as the game master, controlling the monsters and enemies, while the other players fight to survive in the game's famously brutal and unpredictable world. A good tabletop RPG also makes use of miniatures, and this one is no exception: there's a new set releasing in November 2026, and it's called Allies & Enemies.

"Enhance your gameplay of the Dungeon Crawler Carl roleplaying games with these 10 pre-painted Dungeon Crawler Carl miniatures," reads the official product description. "This set features many of the most dangerous and friendly characters from the bestselling LitRPG book series ready to use in your RPG campaigns or simply to collect! Inside you’ll find Brynhild's daughters: Hekla & Eva, Bianca & Prepotente and even Lucia Mar in both her day and night forms!"

Also releasing in November is the Mobs of Mordecai set, and the Unstoppable set, both of which feature their own unique pre-painted miniatures. If you're a fan of Dungeon Crawler Carl, the RPG is absolutely worth checking out. The full game launches November 2026, and the 300-page rulebook is also available to pre-order now.

The Dungeon Crawler Carl Roleplaying Game Core Rulebook is 300+ pages focusing on world dungeon floors 3 to 5. The book talks players through character creation, skills, spells, neighborhoods, saferooms, loot, mobs, and pretty much everything you need to play properly. You can build your own character from the ground up with nearly infinite combinations of backgrounds, skills, races, and classes, so there's plenty of scope for the full Dungeon Crawler Carl experience.

The next Dungeon Crawler Carl book, currently under the working title The Beautiful Place, doesn't have an official release date at the time of writing, but this RPG and its various sets of minatures should keep you happy until it arrives.

#3437. Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

#3436. These Costco-Exclusive Big-Screen Hisense TVs Drop Under $1,000 for Members This Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Black Friday is bringing some substantial discounts on big-screen TVs this year, particularly for Costco members looking to upgrade without spending well over $1,000. From November 26 through November 30, the retailer is dropping the 100-inch Hisense QD7 to $999 from $1,799, an $800 discount, while the 85-inch Hisense U65 Pro will also cost $999, down from $1,299. Both models are Costco exclusives, and come with a three-year Allstate protection plan, bringing the total coverage to five years when combined with the manufacturer’s warranty.

For anyone who puts sheer size first, the 100-inch QD7 offers an enormous viewing area for movies, sports, and gaming, with a 4K Hi-QLED display that uses Quantum Dot technology to produce richer, more vibrant colors. It's particularly appealing for a spacious living room or dedicated entertainment area, though you'll want to measure your wall and seating distance before committing to a screen this large. As for performance, the 85-inch QD7 offers a useful reference point, since CNET named it one of the best 85-inch TVs of 2026—and the two models share the same features apart from screen size.

The 85-inch U65 Pro, meanwhile, gives up 15 inches of screen space but adds Mini-LED backlighting with local dimming for better contrast and more controlled highlights, particularly in darker movie scenes. The latter is particularly worth considering, having earned an "outstanding" rating and an Editors' Choice award from PCMag.

Ultimately, the choice comes down to whether you'd prefer the extra screen space of the QD7 or the more advanced picture technology of the U65 Pro. Either way, these Black Friday discounts make a big-screen upgrade considerably more affordable for Costco members.

#3434. ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.]

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”

Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

The finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke said. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”

But Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”

“That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke said. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”

In Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”

“We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”

“The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke said. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other big finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

“The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo said. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”

“Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he said, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”

Throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

“Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke said. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”

“But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”

One way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

“The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke said. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo said. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be announced is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

#3432. Xbox Game Pass Officially Makes 10/10 RPG Trilogy 100% Free

There are plenty of genuinely excellent video game trilogies. I'm partial to the Batman Arkham trilogy myself, and I also have a lot of time for the first three Halo games. Dark Souls is also a solid trifecta, regardless of what some people say about the middle chapter. Oh, and Assassin's Creed gave Ezio a perfect trilogy back in the day. However, when it comes to truly perfect video game trilogies, I'd argue one stands out above all the others. And it just so happens to be free via Xbox Game Pass.

Back in 2007, the first in what would become a new trilogy emerged for Xbox 360. The journey finally concluded in 2012, because back then it was normal to get more than one game in a franchise per decade. It was a simpler time. Fast-forward to 2021, and the definitive way to experience this trilogy was released, and is now available at no extra cost with Xbox Game Pass Ultimate.

I truly believe that Mass Effect is gaming's greatest trilogy. Sure, Mass Effect 3 kind of screws things up at the eleventh hour, but it's a minor dent in what is otherwise one of the most ambitious, epic RPG experiences in video game history. Over the course of three games, players can carry their very own Commander Shepard through an interstellar conflict, with their choices, romances, and allies carrying through the games. Friends live or die based on your decisions, and the fate of the galaxy is entirely in your hands. Alternatively, you could just spend all your time trying to hook up with the attractive blue alien. It's your call.

Mass Effect Legendary Edition is undoubtedly the best way to play this trilogy in 2026. With improved graphics and refined gameplay, it streamlines the experience across all three games. It also contains all the original DLC, including Mass Effect 2's Lair of the Shadow Broker, which remains one of the greatest story expansions ever made.

But what really sets Mass Effect apart from the competition is its world building and relationships. After all, what would be the point in us having a persistent character across all three games if the relationships were all utterly dull? Every single member of Shepard's crew across the saga is a fully fleshed-out character with their own goals, their own views on the unfolding conflicts, and their own issues to overcome. Working out who to ally yourself with and, sometimes, who to let die, makes for gut-wrenching storytelling.

We know that Mass Effect 5 is coming at some point (although it might be a while), so if you've ever wondered what all the fuss is about, this is the perfect opportunity to dive in to one of the best RPG series ever made. Heck, if you start Mass Effect now, you'll definitely have rolled credits on Mass Effect 3 by the time GTA 6 comes out and devours everyone's spare time. You can then also see for yourself that the ending to Mass Effect 3 is nowhere near as bad as people made it out to be at the time.

#3431. 23 Years Later, Billy Bob Thornton’s Holiday Crime Masterpiece Is Officially a Streaming Hit

"Is [insert film] a Christmas movie?" is a long-running (and perhaps somewhat tiresome) debate in our modern culture. This question often applies to dark, gritty, and R-rated movies that just happen to take place during the holiday season, but share little resemblance to the magic and wonder of Miracle on 34th Street, i.e. the preeminent target of this debate, Die Hard. But for the Christmas movie purists, the hardest to embrace might be a film that unquestionably fits the bill for the genre: Bad Santa.

Crude, profane, and cynical aren't what you expect (or likely want) from the festive season, but the enduring 2003 black comedy, starring Billy Bob Thornton as the worst mall Santa your kid could ever meet, reflects the dark side of Christmas that lingers over many people. Before becoming one of the biggest stars on 2020s television, Thornton delivered one of the most hilarious performances in Terry Zwigoff's intimate portrait of depression and loneliness — a film that got lumped in with, but should absolutely not be confused with the other raunchy comedies of the 2000s. And with it currently charting among Paramout+'s top 10 most-streamed movies, it's a great time for a reevaluation.

2003 gave us two classic holiday films that capture both sides of the Christmas movie coin. Flip it, and you'll either land on Elf or Bad Santa. While both vary tonally and thematically, they each represented the modern direction of the Christmas movie by grounding the stakes and focusing on oddball and outsider characters interacting with the contemporary world. However, the world had never seen anything quite like what co-writers Glenn Ficarra and John Requa had cooking in the fireplace. As hackneyed as an R-rated movie about a pair of degenerate con artists who pose as Santa and an elf to rob department stores may sound, the assured, countercultural direction of Terry Zwigoff and a tour de force performance by Billy Bob Thornton, who cemented his screen persona as the unscrupulous curmudgeon, turned Bad Santa into an unexpected holiday masterpiece.

The poster and log-line of Bad Santa suggests that the film belongs to the lineage of raunchy gross-out comedies of the "Frat Pack," made by the likes of Will Ferrell, Ben Stiller, and Vince Vaughn. In reality, the movie is less like There's Something About Mary and more linked to Zwigoff's provocative character studies, notably Crumb and Ghost World. While the film is undoubtedly a laugh riot filled with copious amounts of profanity, sexual hijinks, alcohol consumption, and sociopathic behavior, it ultimately has a dramatic tenor that is totally earned. Thornton leans into the misanthropy of Willie, a career criminal who is simultaneously conducting his next big score with his partner, Marcus (Tony Cox), and chaperoning a shy and neglected kid (Brett Kelly) who has unexpectedly come into his life. Unlike Ebenezer Scrooge, there is no redeeming Willie, whose sadness is rooted in such dark pockets of his soul that the main goal is just to make sure he doesn't destroy everything around him.

"You see, George, you've really had a wonderful life."

For many, Willie could be a relatable character (or at least the Willie who doesn't break the law or violate basic moral principles). His overwhelming melancholy, alienation, and disinterest in engaging with the pageantry of Christmas festivities matches the seasonal depression that many suffer from during this time of joy and celebration. Beyond Willie, everyone in Bad Santa has a case of the holiday blues, as even the kids and parents waiting in line to sit on Santa's lap appear embittered and ambivalent. The Arizona setting, which could trick a Northerner into thinking it was the 4th of July, also melts away the cozy Christmas spirit. Willie's unexpected friend, an inscrutable kid named Thurman, is entranced by Christmas, even if he doesn't have the emotional capability to celebrate its wonder. Bad Santa is a study of lonely outcasts looking for a purpose.

Bad Santa punches above its weight class thanks to high-level performances, impeccable craft, and bold tonal balance. Acting alongside Billy Bob Thornton and matching his acidic humor is the late Bernie Mac as the mall's head of security, who wants a cut of Willie's heist. Even at its most harsh, Bad Santa will make you laugh through the sheer irreverence displayed on the screen, as there are few things funnier than Thornton tarnishing the sanctity of Santa Claus. The film never shies away from raunch and broadly mean-spirited humor, but on repeat viewings, it's easier to appreciate Zwigoff's sincere examination of depression and loneliness (the director's cut expands on the film's dramatic beats and tones down the slapstick). The movie is far more than just a cheap premise about an NSFW St. Nick, and it speaks to the blurred line between holiday cheer and winter blues.
