#3429. Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.]

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

When you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone said to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

So, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

#3428. 8 Classic PlayStation Games That Are Barely Playable Today

If you’ve ever watched someone play an old PlayStation game and wondered why their character keeps spinning around in circles, congratulations, you’ve already met tank controls. If you’re unfamiliar, here’s your quick introduction: With tank controls, pressing up moves your character forward in whatever direction they’re facing, and pressing left or right only rotates them, so with the stick alone, you can’t sidestep or turn on a dime. That’s manageable in a hallway. It’s much less so when you’re sneaking past a guard, lining up a shot, or timing a leap across a pit, which is why the same scheme caused trouble in just about every genre during the PS1 era. These eight classic games are the hardest to go back to, whether the culprit is tank controls or something else entirely.

The dealbreaker: Lining up one jump means turning in place, backing up, taking a run-up, and holding a grab button in midair. Every single time

Reminder: Tomb Raider is a platformer. You’re jumping roughly every 15 seconds, and most of those jumps demand precision measured in single pixels. The tank controls were supposed to help players thread that needle, but they also meant holding down a series of buttons in a specific order at perfectly timed moments, every few seconds, over the course of a whole game. Here’s what a “big” jump looked like in practice: Walk to the edge, hop back once, run forward, jump at the last second, and hold the grab button while in the air. All while counting the number of blocks you’re jumping around and using specific button combinations for standing, running, and walking jumps. If you guess wrong, game over.

The good news is that Aspyr’s 2024 remaster lets you switch to modern controls, with the camera on the right stick, or keep the classic scheme if you’re feeling brave. A full remake, Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, will be released in February 2027. In the meantime, take comfort in the one polite thing Lara does: she’ll never walk off an edge, though she’ll happily run directly off one.

The dealbreaker: A fear meter instead of a health bar, and a game that punishes you for running out of ammo.

In a shooter, running out of ammo is a special kind of stressful. Here, you’ll follow three mercenaries as they chase a supernatural conspiracy through Hong Kong in 2050. What starts as a job to retrieve a Triad boss’s daughter turns into a descent into a surreal version of hell, with Triads, zombies, and demons along your journey. Get spotted or take a hit, and your character’s fear will climb. Helpfully, so will the danger you’re dodging. Fear Effect uses tank controls, which trap you more often than they allow you to run. A 2025 re-release from Limited Run Games made the tank controls optional, and added widescreen, rewind, and save states. It’s maybe the nicest thing anyone has done for tank controls: Made them optional.

The dealbreaker: A zombie in the next room, and a camera angle that can’t see it.

Not being able to see a threat lurking around the corner is possibly the point; it does heighten the terror in this game significantly. Resident Evil helped define the survival horror genre, and the fixed camera angles are part of that. You steer Jill or Chris, two members of the Raccoon City police’s elite S.T.A.R.S. unit who get trapped in a mansion infested with zombies, with tank controls — which means “forward” always means forward for the character, regardless of the camera angle you’re working in. That consistency helps when the view cuts every time you cross a doorway, but combat suffers, since you’re lining up shots at things you often can’t see. Your stiff, complex movements don’t help either.

If you want the original experience, the Director’s Cut, which adds analog stick support, is available on PS Plus Premium. If you want the best way to play the first game, though, the 2002 remake (and its 2015 HD remaster) features a rebuilt mansion with new graphics, lighting, and revised layouts.

The dealbreaker: You can look in first person, but you can’t shoot in it.

This is the kind of thing that sounds like a minor detail until you’re trying to sneak past a guard. Snake, a legendary soldier pulled out of retirement to infiltrate a remote Alaskan nuclear weapons facility, can switch to a first-person view to scout. But when you need to aim, you’re back in the top-down camera, often at an angle that doesn’t show you the person you’re trying to shoot. This is a stealth game where the stealth mechanic is extremely unforgiving. The sequels get a bit better, fortunately. If you’re interested in giving the original a go, it’s playable in Master Collection Vol. 1 on PC, PS5, Switch, and Xbox Series X. Even though it’s unwieldy, at least it’s short: you can finish it in a handful of hours.

The dealbreaker: “DANGER!” prompts that take your controls away at the worst possible moment

Clearly, this is a recipe for disaster. The setup here is delightfully silly: You’ve got a secret research island, a missing scientist, and a government project that has gone very wrong. (Spoilers: There are dinosaurs involved.) Imagine Resident Evil, but with dinosaurs, and you’ll get the right idea. You play as Regina, a special ops agent on a mission to rescue a scientist named Dr. Kirk. Tragically for the doctor, you move with tank controls under a camera that follows you instead of staying fixed.

Capcom tried to mitigate this with a quick-turn button, but Dino Crisis takes your controls away exactly when you’d want them most. At scripted points of the game, that “DANGER!” prompt flashes on screen, during which surviving means button mashing, not steering. Everything you’ve carefully practiced, your turning, aiming, and running skills instantly become irrelevant, and if your reactions aren’t fast enough, you’re punished.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The dealbreaker: Armored enemies, and a very slow manual aim

A shooter lives or dies depending on how fast you can land headshots. Syphon Filter is Sony’s stealth-and-shooting spy thriller, starring secret agent Gabe Logan. Gabe’s job is to stop a deadly virus, and the game wants you to play it like a fast-paced spy movie. If only that were possible! It’s not quite tank controls, but Syphon Filter is very unresponsive and awkward to play. You see this most when you try to shoot. The game does give you lock-on aiming, but that doesn’t help when your enemy is wearing body armor…so you need to switch to a slower first-person aim, anyway, to go for the head. So the skill the game cares about the most, landing a headshot on an armored guard, is the one it makes you do slowest. While enemies shoot you from off-screen. Have fun with that!

The dealbreaker: A role-playing sequel that swapped turn-based battles for real-time shooting, with controls so stiff that learning them is the hardest boss

This is a strange reinvention for a series that started as a turn-based RPG. Aya Brea, a former NYPD officer, now works for an FBI unit that hunts creatures created by mutated cells. In the sequel, she fights in real time, with tank-style controls. You explore pre-rendered backgrounds, lock on to enemies, and dodge as you investigate a monster outbreak that starts in a Los Angeles shopping tower and leads to a deserted town in Nevada. The toughest part of Parasite Eve 2 isn’t a boss or a random encounter but mastering what one contemporary reviewer called “the stiff and stubborn playcontrol,” though it gets easier after an hour or two. That’s the good news. The bad news is that you still have to spend that hour or two developing that muscle memory.

The dealbreaker: It’s very difficult to find on modern consoles, and the original code got lost

Now this is a different kind of unplayable. For the original Silent Hill, access to the actual game is your main enemy, not necessarily the odd controls or unforgiving gameplay. Here, you’re playing as a man searching a fog-covered town for his missing daughter. The 1999 game itself is out of reach on modern consoles: its publisher has acknowledged that the source code was lost, so for a very long time it couldn’t be officially ported or remastered. (A fan decompilation project just finished reconstructing the original code, which could open the door to unofficial ports someday.) Your options for playing this today are an original PS1 disc or, for now, the PS3 store.

If you want the series on a modern console in the meantime, there’s the Silent Hill 2 remake, Silent Hill f from 2025, and Townfall. For now, the best way to play the first Silent Hill is a PlayStation, a disc, and a lot — a lot — of patience for dealing with fog.

A new gaming reality was virtually within sight

#3426. How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino said in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report says that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting new sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV shows, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3425. Ridley Scott's 8-Episode Sci-Fi Thriller Is An S-Tier Cyberpunk Show

It took a while for Ridley Scott’s most iconic sci-fi franchise to reach the small screen, but Hulu’s Alien streaming series exceeded expectations when the show did arrive in 2025. The Alien franchise has lived many lives since director Ridley Scott’s original sci-fi horror blockbuster was released in 1979. Director James Cameron’s 1986 sequel Aliens upped the action quotient of the franchise, downplaying the horror elements in the process.

While Aliens was the most action-packed of the Alien movies, 1992’s divisive Alien 3 took the exact opposite approach. Grim, downbeat, and dour, future Se7en director David Fincher’s sequel was certainly dark and disturbing, but lacked the fun and thrills of Alien and Aliens. 1997’s Alien: Resurrection was something of a course correction, but Scott’s prequels Prometheus and Alien: Covenant divided the franchise’s large fan base further.

Even without mentioning the dubious canon of the Alien Vs Predator movies, the Alien franchise is one with vertiginous highs and embarrassingly misguided lows. As such, it is no surprise that the first Alien streaming series came laden with decades of hype and high expectations. What was surprising is the fact that Fargo show runner Noah Hawley’s Hulu series Alien: Earth managed to not only live up to, but even exceed these expectations with its subversive, spooky sci-fi storytelling.

Taking place after the events of Prometheus and Alien: Covenant, Alien: Earth followed 2024’s theatrical reboot Alien: Romulus with a story that offered a fresh perspective on the franchise. Alien and Aliens had supporting characters, like Ash and Bishop, who turned out to be Weyland-Yutani Corporation’s cyborgs, while Prometheus and Alien: Romulus had lead characters who were synthetic humans in David and Andy.

However, Alien: Earth’s intriguing spin on the Alien franchise mythology was the show’s decision to focus primarily on hybrid characters, synthetic bodies that had real human consciousnesses transferred into them. While there were human characters too, Hawley’s show spent most of its time with these synthetic “Lost Boys” as they navigated the disastrous escape of one of the Weyland-Yutani Corporation’s Xenomorphs.

Scott returned as an executive producer on Alien: Earth, but Hawley is the creator and showrunner and the Hulu show benefited dramatically from his loose approach to existing franchise lore and canon. As the USCSS Maginot brings back samples of extraterrestrial life to Earth for the Corporation’s top-secret experiments, this process exposes the main characters to the lethal Xenomorph, as well as a shady conspiracy involving their infamously shadowy employers.

Since Alien: Earth has a far longer runtime than any of the movies in the franchise, the show could explore the world of the series in more depth and detail than ever before. Much like Netflix’s ambitious sci-fi series 3 Body Problem. Alien: Earth spares no expense in creating an immersive reality that looks as lush and cinematic as any big-screen genre outing.

While Prime Video’s The Peripheral and Netflix’s Altered Carbon were similarly ambitious cyberpunk shows, both critically acclaimed series were canceled in their prime before they could fully fulfill their potential. The Peripheral lasted one eight-episode season on the streaming service, while Altered Carbon made it to a mere two seasons before the adaptation was axed.

In recent years, Prime Video’s expensive spinoff Blade Runner 2099 and Apple TV’s upcoming William Gibson adaptation Neuromancer have hinted at an openness to exploring the cyberpunk genre on the small screen once again. However, no matter how well these shows do, Ridley Scott’s Hulu spinoff Alien: Earth will always deserve credit for pioneering this trend as Noah Hawley’s cyberpunk show expanded the sparsely seen setting of the Alien movies into a lived-in world.

#3424. 47 Years Later, This Remains The Most Addictive Sci-Fi Franchise of All Time

In this day and age, franchise films have overwhelmed the cultural landscape, but one still finds a way to reinvent itself. This IP continues to impress, even decades after it came screaming out of the darkness. Sci-fi horror was in its early days in the ‘70s, but Ridley Scott’s Alien redefined what it meant to be scared.

Starring Sigourney Weaver, the first Alien film was a jarring flip on the script. Instead of slasher films that often victimized women, the pendulum swung the other way. Weaver stars as Ripley, an officer on the spaceship Nostromo who is really the only person concerned when an alien lifeform is found. Instead of adhering to the quarantine protocols, Captain Dallas (Tom Skerritt) brings an infected crew member on board, which allows the Xenomorph to be born — literally and painfully. Alien shows sexual violence pointed at men instead of women, and this first film fueled a sci-fi franchise that continues to impress audiences.

The heart of the Alien films is the “perfect organism” that has been terrorizing viewers since 1979. This concept is what makes the series so addictive — and why the Weyland-Yutani corporation continues to try and capture the ultimate predator for profit. Alien has always been a source of fascination for viewers in the theaters, even with the less-than-popular franchise films. Following Sigourney Weaver’s tenure as Ellen Ripley, the series continued with some unfairly criticized sequels.

Prometheus served as a divisive prequel to the franchise, co-written by Lost co-showrunner Damon Lindelof. Viewers took issue with the Engineers, but the origins of the Xenomorph were still a captivating story. Starring Noomi Rapace, Charlize Theron, and Idris Elba, Prometheus shows the challenges of looking for faith in all the wrong places.

For some, the film was a misfire, but like the Xenomorph, the franchise always returned. Recent additions, such as Alien: Romulus, capitalized on what made the franchise so enduring to begin with. A love letter to the series, Romulus, takes place between Alien and Aliens as a crew imprisoned by Weyland-Yutani gets trapped in another version of Ripley’s story. Horror director Fede Álvarez finds the sweet spot with the film, showing the heartbreaking reality of an android with the character Andy (David Jonsson) and a killer third act – in more ways than one.

It was with FX’s television series, Alien: Earth, that really showed how to do a franchise right. The series elevated the original concept of a victim stuck in a room with a killing machine and broadened the concept even further. Created by Fargo scribe Noah Hawley, the series is set a couple of years before the first Alien film.

At its core, Alien has always been a criticism of capitalism, which Hawley’s series explores. At a time when technology has reached its peak, corporations have been looking for a path to immortality. Humanity has created cyborgs, fully synthetic life, and hybrids. This sets up the main conflict when a research ship crashes into Earth, carrying a deadly secret.

Alien: Earth is just another way to explore the themes set up in Alien with even more specificity. This franchise continues to draw in viewers not just because of the scares, but also because of the social commentary that was always part of the IP’s DNA. Alien defined sci-fi horror and continues to show others in the genre how it's done.

Humanity’s most nightmarish invader, the Xenomorph, has stalked moviegoers for over four decades, thrusting us into claustrophobic terror aboard derelict spaceships, brutal colony excursions, and existential laboratory nightmares. Ellen Ripley becomes a relentless warrior across film series that blend horror, action, and cosmic dread. Prequels like Prometheus dig into bioweapon origins, while modern installments such as Alien: Romulus and the TV spinoff Alien: Earth expand the mythos with synthetic humans and corporate chaos.

#3422. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

Amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3421. 7 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Food

Anything can be the star of a Far Side comic. While most of them featured stupid humans or talking animals as their main characters, the surrealist streak in cartoonist Gary Larson sometimes gave life to inanimate objects as well. For example, there’s a strip where a jogger tells a living pair of scissors that they can no longer run together. And if scissors can be alive in The Far Side comics, just about anything can, including food.

Here are the seven funniest Far Side comics that star food, some of which feature food that has even gained sentience for the sake of a perfect joke.

I love this comic strip because it is just unabashedly silly. Not only are sandwiches alive in this one-panel reality, but they have such a complex social structure that they even have their own organized crime. The sandwich mafia is so cruel that it punishes its victims by hurling them into a pit of fourth-graders. If I were the sandwich, I’d be especially worried about the fourth-grader in the green stripey shirt. He looks vicious.

Yet another food item that has turned to a life of crime. Here, Larson interprets potato salad going bad in the silliest way possible​​​​​​​.

This is a twist on that classic gag where, with two people in a life boat, one begins to imagine the other as food. This one features​​​​​​​ a man and a cow in a lifeboat​​​​​​​, so the man naturally imagines steak while looking at the cow​​​​​​​. As for the cow, well, he dreams of the man as a pile of man-shaped grass.

I love how adorable-looking these man-eating bears are as they stumble upon a group of campers in sleeping bags and exclaim “Sandwiches!” Personally, I think of sleeping bags as more burrito-like or even more like pita bread than sandwiches, but perhaps these bears aren’t terribly educated about the ways other cultures eat.

One of the reasons why The Far Side endures more than 30 years after Gary Larson concluded his strip is that he never spoke down to his audience. Sure, he had some dumb jokes sometimes, but they were never dumbed down for our sake; they were just dumb​​​​​​​ for the sake of being dumb — like a sandwich mafia. Larson could pull off the lowbrow and the highbrow, often in the very same comic, as this one illustrates​​​​​​​.

At a glance, it doesn’t even seem like there’s a joke here, despite the simple caption​​​​​​​: “Soup of the day is ready!” This is one of those comic strips by Larson that demands that you go looking for the punchline. Larson seems to trust that the audience will find the joke (or maybe he doesn’t care if some don’t, which I applaud). Eventually, you see that this chef is missing his shoe, meaning he used it to make the soup. So for all that highbrow thinking you had to do to find the punchline, the joke is incredibly lowbrow. It’s the perfect mix.

Larson also got into really dark humor at times. He once drew a comic strip where a snake killed himself by becoming his own noose, which is both silly and incredibly macabre. Yet this food-centric panel is so dark that it borders on creepy. Who is this guy that wants to buy this young employee of the butcher? And who is this butcher that is willing to sell him?

I first read this comic strip when I was a teenager, around the time when I first discovered The Far Side and quickly became obsessed with it. Since then, every time I make a waffle, I cannot help but think of this comic strip. I’ll mix the batter, spray the waffle iron, pour the mix in, close the top, and wait for that little light to go off. Inevitably, as I’m staring at that little light, I’ll murmur, “Slave to the waffle light.” It's one of those pieces of art that just speaks to a real-life truism.

When making waffles, we are all Wendell Zurkowitz.

#3419. All 32 Episodes Of HBO’s Crime Masterpiece Deliver A Masterclass In Blending Genres

HBO's Barry delivers a masterclass in blending genres, between its hitman premise, comedic tone, and psychological thriller elements. It's also incredibly easy to binge with 32 sharply paced episodes, and is one of HBO's all-time great modern series with 10 Emmy wins and a near-perfect 98% Rotten Tomatoes score. Featuring performances by Bill Hader, Stephen Root, Henry Winkler, Sarah Goldberg, and more, Barry belongs in the same elite category as Veep, Curb Your Enthusiasm, and The Righteous Gemstones as one of the most prolific HBO comedy series ever made.

Few series available to stream on HBO Max blend various distinct genres as masterfully as Barry, which primarily combines dark comedy with crime drama and psychological thriller. Bill Hader stars as the titular protagonist Barry Berkman, a professional hitman who is sent on a contract killer assignment to Los Angeles, only to end up falling in love with the craft of acting. The former Marine-turned-assassin takes an acting class taught by Gene Cousineau (Winkler) and is enamored by the idea of escaping his own identity by assuming those of fictional characters. While Barry continues to work as a hitman, he gets a new lease on life by throwing himself into the world of acting.

Several key supporting characters also challenge the traditional expectations within the crime genre, specifically Anthony Carrigan's NoHo Hank, who is simultaneously a serious but hilarious member of an organized crime operation. Barry and NoHo Hank defy the norms of the standard criminal characters seen in countless crime series, which makes Barry a triumph of genre-blending technique. What's more, the series itself rests on its contrasting tone of crime and comedy, while also diving into Barry's psychological profile as a hitman with a moral compass, which exacerbates his repressed personal feelings of guilt. These elements elevate the series beyond a simple crime comedy.

Barry is a series worth investing in on HBO Max because it truly does get better and more complex with each new season without ever sacrificing the qualities that made its debut season such an instant success. By the time Barry reaches its third season, which earned a perfect 100% Rotten Tomatoes score and is often considered the best of the series, it reaches new heights in terms of both story and character development, especially in how the past comes to affect Barry and his growing ambitions to correct his previous mistakes. The psychological elements become more integral in the narrative, while the series also hits impressive achievements as an action thriller.

All 50 episodes of Apple TV's space sci-fi masterpiece deliver an extraordinary alternate-history adventure that's perfect from start to finish.

Hader also evolved as a visual storyteller and director in Barry's final season, taking complete creative control of the series by directing all eight episodes while also remaining its star. Through Hader's lens, the unconventional crime-comedy hybrid develops into a full-bodied psychological drama that touches on darker and deeper themes than the debut season, including Barry's relationship with violence and the myriad ways in which he has altered his identity, lied to himself, and hurt other people. Because of this, Barry delivers a phenomenal showcase of not only how to pull off a genre-blending series, but how to utilize various genres to enhance the show's original premise.

#3418. How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

#3416. 10 Years Later, Netflix's Greatest Sci-Fi Masterpiece Has Officially Racked Up 1.4B Streaming Hours

Netflix's catalog is full of memorable shows, but even after 10 years, one series still stands above the rest. Stranger Things kicked off a massive franchise for the streamer, delivering terrifying mysteries, lovable characters, and a heavy dose of nostalgia. Since its 2016 premiere, the sci-fi show has become one of Netflix's most recognizable properties. Although the series finale aired at the end of last year, Stranger Things has continued to draw an audience throughout 2026, with fans watching more than 1.4 billion hours, and it's easy to see why.

Stranger Things' five seasons have their share of ups and downs, most notably the divided reaction to the finale, but 2026's viewing numbers show just how much love fans still have. By following a supernatural mystery that threatens the small town of Hawkins, Indiana, and the unlikely group that forms to stop it, Stranger Things blends horror with coming-of-age drama — an irresistible combination that's only one of the reasons why the show continues to endure on streaming a year after its original ending.

Over the last decade, Stranger Things has been impossible to avoid because of its undeniable cultural impact. The Netflix series thrives as a nostalgic '80s mystery that draws people in quickly, but soon reveals a story that isn't so easily defined by one genre. With lighthearted moments of friendship between the main characters, murder mysteries, and villains straight out of a horror movie, the show appeals to a broad audience. From middle school bullying to government conspiracies, the story's unpredictability is one of Stranger Things' major strengths. Each season delivers more mysteries, starting with Will Byers' (Noah Schnapp) disappearance from Hawkins and growing to include Eleven's (Millie Bobby Brown) background and the looming threat of Vecna (Jamie Campbell Bower).

Stranger Things ultimately thrives by raising the stakes. The town's safety is at risk, and from Season 1 onward, the show makes it clear that not everyone is safe. Throughout the series, fan-favorite characters are killed off permanently, providing real consequences for the story, and these emotional losses make fans want to return to the series and revisit their favorites. With its major twists and heart-wrenching moments, Stranger Things' story is so intriguing that fans are clearly struggling to say goodbye to the show forever.

Although the series has plenty to offer in its storytelling, Stranger Things' greatest strength is its characters. The series has a huge cast, and many have become fan favorites, but the core group is where the story thrives. Eleven, Mike (Finn Wolfhard), Will, Dustin (Gaten Matarazzo), Lucas (Caleb McLaughlin), and Max (Sadie Sink) are the heart of the narrative as their friendship grows and changes, and the team they form, as well as the older characters who join them, add the necessary humor and heart.

Stranger Things would never have gained so much attention without its lovable characters, and it continues to develop them thoughtfully as the story unfolds — focusing on elements like Eleven's self-discovery, Hopper's (David Harbour) grief, and Steve Harrington's (Joe Keery) transformation from a self-centered teen to a loyal protector. These character arcs add depth to the series and are best seen through rewatching the entire series.

Stranger Things is one of the most influential shows of the last decade, and it clearly still holds that distinction. Based on the viewing numbers, fans continue to return to the original Netflix series, which has spawned a franchise that includes the spin-off Stranger Things: Tales from '85, a stage play, and several tie-in novels that expand the story. Stranger Things may have ended last year, but with so many dedicated fans still watching, it's not going away any time soon.

#3415. ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

”The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” stands on its own as a beautifully written (by Quentin Tarantino) and directed (by David Fincher) Los Angeles noir that both invites and earns comparison with 1970s classics like “Night Moves” and “The Long Goodbye,” but its rewards increase exponentially the more familiar you are with its predecessor, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Although Fincher and Tarantino have both argued that the movie is less a sequel than simply another Cliff Booth adventure, the movie has quite a few fun Easter eggs to reward fans of Brad Pitt’s first time playing the laid-back stuntman.

Perhaps the most delightful callback to “Once Upon a Time” is the reappearance of two of cowboy actor Rick Dalton’s (Leonardo DiCaprio) collaborators on the “Lancer” pilot that took up a good section of the middle third of Tarantino’s earlier film. Co-star James Stacy (Timothy Olyphant) makes a brief appearance alongside “Lancer” director Sam Wanamaker, played once again by Nicholas Hammond, whose exuberant turn as the real-life actor-director in “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” was one of that film’s greatest pleasures. Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

Hammond’s part is, like the other returning faces from “Once Upon a Time” (aside from Pitt, of course), essentially a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it cameo, but he was delighted to return to Tarantino’s world and to share the screen with Olyphant once again. He first heard rumblings that Wanamaker might return for “Cliff Booth” well over a year ago, when the assumption was that Tarantino would direct the script.

“Quentin has his team, and it’s the same crew that works on all his films,” Hammond told IndieWire. “I’d gotten to know them on ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,’ and a couple of the guys from the crew sent me emails saying, ‘Hey, it’s great we’re going to be working together again.’ Everyone had an ironclad NDA, so no one could tell me anything about the film, but that was my one little clue. Then, of course, when Quentin dropped out, and it looked like the movie was not happening, I thought, ‘There goes that chance.'”

Hammond was elated, therefore, when Pitt resurrected the movie by giving the script to his friend Fincher. “Timothy and I knew that we were coming in basically as an Easter egg,” Hammond said. “It was a tiny scene, and we knew that, but we were just thrilled that we were asked to come back, that Quentin thought it would be cool to have those characters back in the movie again. Let’s face it, he can get any actor he wants in the world to do anything, so it was an honor and a joy even though it’s a tiny little moment in the film.”

When Hammond played Wanamaker in the first film, he saw an opportunity to pay tribute to all the talented, hardworking directors and actors who work in the industry without necessarily becoming A-list names — a category that includes himself. “Your career ebbs and flows,” Hammond said. “You do a lot of small roles on television or small roles in movies, and then you get your own series, or then you get a big movie, and that’s the life of most actors in Hollywood. Even people like Leonardo and Brad say they have tons of friends who were as good as them when they were all starting out, but so much of it depends on if the right role comes along at the right moment.”

Hammond noted that for a lot of actors that moment never comes, but Tarantino has always recognized that that doesn’t make someone any less of an actor. “Most people think that if you’re good, you’re going to become a star. Quentin realizes there are a hell of a lot of very good actors out there who don’t become stars — that there are so many stars that have to align in the universe for that to happen. He admires and celebrates actors like Michael Madsen and Bruce Dern who have been journeyman actors their entire lives with moments of success, or flares of global recognition.”

Hammond experienced one of those flares as a teenager, when he played one of the Von Trapp kids in Robert Wise’s classic musical “The Sound of Music,” and again several years later when he played Peter Parker on the CBS television series “The Amazing Spider-Man” — the role that made Tarantino a lifelong Hammond fan. “I’m fortunate in that way,” Hammond said. “I feel luckier than most actors in my situation, because I’ve had a few goalpost roles that the world is aware of.”

60 years after he made it, Hammond still runs into “Sound of Music” fans all the time. “I was on a plane yesterday flying to Sydney, and a stewardess crouched down next to my seat and said, ‘Nicholas, I just have to let you know that my family watches ‘Sound of Music’ every year,'” Hammond said. “‘When my grandmother was ready to pass away, she said the last thing she wanted was for all of us to gather around the TV together as a family and watch that movie.’ I don’t care how rich you are or how many movies you’ve been in, how many actors get a chance to be in a movie that has that kind of effect on people?”

Hammond says that, having lived through the eras “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and “Cliff Booth” recreate, he knows Tarantino got that period of L.A. history completely right—something he attributes to the writer’s encyclopedic knowledge of his own work and that of all his peers. “There are very few people who could capture the 1970s as accurately as Quentin does,” Hammond said. “It’s his era. He grew up watching me as Peter Parker in ‘Spider-Man,’ and he watched all the episodes of ‘Gunsmoke’ I did, and all the episodes of ‘The Waltons’ and ‘The Brady Bunch.’ There’s not a show I was on that he didn’t see and know about.”

In “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Hammond honored the directors of those episodic series whose names the public has forgotten, though Wanamaker, as an actor, was probably better known than many. When he got the part, Hammond was intent on playing Wanamaker with respect while still delivering on all the comic potential of Tarantino’s conception. “One of my fears when we were doing the film is I did not want Zoe Wanamaker to think we were making fun of her father, because we definitely weren’t,” Hammond said. “He was a very serious actor and a serious theater person.”

Hammond took a deep dive into Wanamaker’s life and career for the part. “Quentin’s office sent me a stack of DVDs of movies that Wanamaker had directed, and movies that he had appeared in,” Hammond said. “I got quite familiar with him. The Globe Theatre exists in England today solely because of him. If it weren’t for Sam Wanamaker petitioning and raising money and basically forcing the British government to authorize the building, the Globe wouldn’t be there. They wanted to build public housing there, and he managed to get a groundswell of support. And now, of course, it’s a huge tourist attraction, and in his honor the smaller studio theater within the building is called the Sam Wanamaker Theater.”

Hammond says he knew he was a part of something special when he saw “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” at its Cannes world premiere. “I’ve been lucky enough to be in three really significant films: [Peter Brook’s] ‘Lord of the Flies,’ ‘The Sound of Music,’ and ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,'” Hammond said. “With three very significant directors. So I’ve had a very fortunate career, and I still get excited just seeing my name on the call sheet. And when you’re working with people like Leo or Timothy Olyphant who are right at the top of their game, they’re the best of the best. I’m on the New York Yankees now, and when I get up to the plate, I better deliver.”

Despite starring in several classics, Hammond is less interested in looking back than in whatever he’s working on now. “I absolutely love being an actor, and I love being on stage. I’ve done a great deal of stage work, and I’m always asked, ‘Which do you like better?’ And the answer always is, whatever I’m doing right then. When I walk into the stage door of a theater, I get exactly the same charge of excitement that I do walking onto a sound stage at a studio. I just feel like I’m home. I feel these are my people. These are the people that I’ve always been the happiest being with since I was 10 years old, and I that will never change.”

Hammond looks to his “Sound of Music” costar Christopher Plummer, who did some of his best work late in life, as a role model. “I’ll do this as long as I possibly can. I’m of the Christopher Plummer philosophy that way,” Hammond said. “The word retirement doesn’t really exist. What would I do? Give up the thing I love the most in the world to play golf? I’m not doing that.”

Kitchen tools become weapons, small wounds can be fatal, and stress will eventually break your mind if left unmanaged. All these elements come together to deliver an authentic and immersive zombie apocalypse experience."

From its promotional images alone, it is clear to see that The Last of Us played a large role in inspiration when it comes to Nakwon: Last Paradise's post-apocalyptic setting. With crumbling buildings, burnt-out cars, and nature reclaiming its domain, these are visuals that are reminiscent of the Naughty Dog title. However, with a more shooter-heavy focus, it is clear that players can expect to cause a lot more chaos in this multiplayer title.

Despite Nakwon: Last Paradise not yet receiving an official release window, those interested will be pleased to learn that the developer has been doing playtests you can request access to. While there isn't currently any word on when the next one will release, you can head over to the official Steam page to check. If a play test is planned, you can click 'Request Access', and you will be notified when the developer is ready to accept new participants.

So, if you are interested in this post-apocalyptic multiplayer shooter with The Last of Us and Tom Clancy's The Division vibes, you will want to add Nakwon: Last Paradise to your Steam wishlist ahead of its full launch. Or don't, it's up to you.
