#3412. Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible

WETA FX has been called upon to do visual effects for everything, from orc armies to superheroes, alien planetscapes to the innards of a whale. On each project, they have to match the movie’s consistency. The goal is to make sure that the VFX blends perfectly into the overall visual style, not so unlike a certain Springfield dad creeping into a hedge.

Meeting that challenge often means the teams at WETA match and then build on live-action footage to get as close to a photorealistic look as possible. But adding digital effects to the wonderful world of stop-motion animation, as with “Wildwood,” WETA FX got to have more fun with creating a world that looks as textured and handmade as the puppets designed and animated by Laika Studios. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

“Everybody was super stoked about this film because it’s so different from what we usually do. People got to be artists,” VFX supervisor Sabine Laimer told IndieWire. “We’re really good at making effects invisible, but here we could actually showcase the artistry. All of our people here loved it.”

This applies to the way that WETA helped intensify battle sequences, the way they expanded sets so that they feel as fast as the impassible woods where most of “Wildwood” takes place, and the way they were able to match cinematographer Caleb Deschanel’s lighting to bring a unity to the digital and puppetry work within individual scenes. When designing the ivy that Alexandra (Carey Mulligan) seeks to control and that Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) seeks to pacify, WETA’s digital leaves weren’t meant to mimic real leaves in nature. They were built to look like the paper leaves a stop motion animator would use.

“[The leaves in ‘Wildwood’] have a different light transmission. They have a different level of detail, depending on how close the camera is to them,” Laimer said. “[We developed] this sort of stage realism, if you want to call it that, rather than realism, and that makes a huge difference.”

One element where WETA needed to heighten the realism most was the ivy, which is eventually summoned into a sentient spire that threatens to overwhelm the entire world. “It’s alive, but it’s not a person. It has character, but it can’t feel like it’s a boss. It has to have intent, but it can’t be so direct that it feels like there’s a brain that’s going after the characters,” VFX supervisor Dan Macarin laid out the challenge of Laika’s brief to IndieWire.

“It had to creep, it had to attack, it had to consume, it had to overgrow,” Laimer added. “There was a lot of material there for us to work with, which was amazing, but we had to translate all of this intricate detail that they’ve built on their practical sets into a digital plinth environment and build it in a way that was malleable for us, and we had different stages of everything.”

Laimer and her team tested ways to mimic the Laika animators’ practical work and drew inspiration from the natural world, like time-lapses of pea shoots with an uncanny, jerky motion as they grow. They built different vignettes that could be placed inside specific shots so the ivy would read as dangerous, but not distract from the drama between the characters. For the moments where the ivy threatens to overwhelm the entire plinth, the WETA team actually used fluid simulation to get the feel of the ivy being like a tsunami, this swelling of constant, growing motion that is headed in a definite direction, not just moving at random.

“We looked at practical references like schools of fish, where they move in unison and create shapes and change directions on purpose. It was a similar thing, or like flocks of starlings in the air. You have to sculpt the [ivy] cyclone per shot so that it’s not distracting in the background, it’s not too busy, but at the same time still feels like it’s alive,” Laimer said.

Hitting that visual effects sweet spot was important in all the visual effects collaborations between WETA and Laika. The path to do that always ran through story, and what visuals would make the storytelling the most immediately legible to the audience. “WETA is really, really fantastic at doing third act battles,” Macarin said. “We’ve done a tremendous number of them over the years and decades, and so it’s not the scope that we have to worry about. We can handle all of that. It’s always, ‘How do we tell this story?’”

In the case of “Wildwood,” telling the story with visual effects meant simplifying a lot, so that even when we placed it behind the explosion of cannon fire (where it would never be safe for a practical camera to go), we still cared about the characters. “We were able to create aesthetic choices that still allow the audience to engage in the battle, but not necessarily put you suddenly into this photorealistic explosion or feel. This is a very colorful, emotionally driven sequence that just happens to have a battle around it,” Macarin said.

The most fantastical-seeming choices in “Wildwood” are all about character. “They shot everything with two suns,” Laimer said. “They had a smaller, sharper key light and then a softer, wider one, which created this really beautiful falloff on the faces that we had to create digitally. That was really cool.”

Getting to build expressive, beautiful worlds in animation — whether digital, stop-motion, or a combination of the two — usually is pretty cool, to be fair. And clearly, in the case of “Wildwood,” it brings out some of WETA’s best work.

#3410. 7 Dystopian Books To Read if You Love 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping'

Beatriz (Bea) Valero de Urquia is a Books & Literature author at Collider, where she focuses on Lists surrounding recent bestsellers, classical novels, and everything in between. She is a historian by training and a bilingual reader, moving between English and Spanish literature.   Beatriz began her career as a technology writer at a startup in the UK. Almost a decade later, journalism has taken her to five cities across three continents and into business reporting, cultural criticism, and live TV commentary. She joined Collider in 2026.  Beatriz has a passion for travelling and loves keeping an eye on the books headed to the screen. One of her favorite pastimes is critiquing the historical accuracy of period movies. She also once volunteered for the Charles Dickens Museum. Beatriz also has a core belief that a book is always better than the movie, but she has been happy to have been proven wrong in a couple of occasions.

When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research. She enjoys tracing family trees for her history and genealogy TikTok, creating databases for historical analysis and sifting through 17th-century stories for the novel she is currently in the process of writing.

Dystopias are back. The genre that took over an entire generation of young readers in the early 2010s is making a return, with the premiere of the movie adaptation of Suzanne Collins' Sunrise on the Reaping, the second prequel novel to The Hunger Games franchise, as well as the release of The Sixth Faction, a new alternate-universe book in Veronica Roth's Divergent series. These stories are entertaining adventures that follow a hero's journey, but they also include political commentary about propaganda and authoritarian states.

Suzanne Collins might be the best-known modern dystopian author, but the genre encompasses hundreds of other great stories. The books below, from cult classics to recent bestsellers and from YA to adult fiction, share their commentary on the impact of propaganda and discussions of young people's futures being sacrificed by the systems meant to protect them. If you walked out of Sunrise on the Reaping wanting more, start here.

In about 200 pages, Belgian author Jacqueline Harpman tells the story of a girl who has grown up in a cage, accompanied by 39 women and surrounded by male guards, who watch them day and night. She does not remember how or why she is there. No one else does either. One day, an alarm goes off, and the guards flee, leaving the door open. The women are able to escape, but find themselves in a deserted world, with no one else around and no information about what has happened. The book shows that the shortest stories can sometimes be the most hard-hitting.

This story would be the equivalent of Haymitch waking up in the middle of the arena, with no clue about how he got there and why. I Who Have Never Known Men's unanswered questions make the reading experience much more powerful. It's a story that questions who humans are and what their purpose is, under the guise of a story with a dystopian environment. Much like the tributes in the Hunger Games arena, the women in this universe seek to hold on to their humanity, even when the society around them has collapsed. Nonetheless, readers coming from Panem should expect a slower, stranger, and more haunting book.

Far from the Hunger Games, Neal Shusterman envisions a world with no hunger. Humanity is at peace and has ended disease and misery. The world even has no death and, instead, this society has tasked scythes with ending people's lives to prevent overpopulation. Citra and Rowan are two teenagers apprenticing for this terrible yet seemingly vital role. Only one will be chosen at the end, and the winner's task is much bleaker than either imagined.

Much like Haymitch's arena, the world of Scythe looks perfect at first. However, its deathless society soon shows its flaws. The book shows a Scythedom split between those who kill out of duty and those who enjoy it. The story then turns into an examination of power, who has it and whom it corrupts. For a book about death, it is much less bloody than some of the titles on this list. However, its reflections are no less meaningful.

Sometimes violence is eerily quiet. This is the path chosen in Kazuo Ishiguro's acclaimed novel Never Let Me Go. It is perhaps a surprising choice for fans of Sunrise on the Reaping, but Ishiguro's book features a similar theme: a society that has agreed that certain children are expendable. Instead of a spectacle, however, this world hides its abuse of children behind the polished doors of a boarding school named Hailsham.

Kathy is much older than most heroes on this list. At 31 years old, she lives in an alternative 1990s England and has been a carer for 11 years. In the novel, she relives the memories of her time at Hailsham, where she was raised by guardians who encouraged her to be creative and stay healthy. Kathy's childhood friends, Ruth and Tommy, grew up together believing in a world of possibility. They eventually learn the terrible truth: the students are actually clones created to donate their organs when needed. There is no rebellion, only the quiet desperation of a life that is not one's own. Shortlisted for the Booker Prize and adapted into a 2010 movie starring Carey Mulligan, Andrew Garfield, and Keira Knightley, it's one of the most heartbreaking books on this list, from a writer who later won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Let's go to Ancient Rome in space — kind of. A version where people are divided by color, marking their class and career. At 16 years old, Darrow is a Red and a miner, living deep beneath the surface of Mars. He believes they are waiting underground until the planet becomes habitable. When his wife, Eo, is hanged for singing a forbidden song, Darrow learns that the Golds have actually been living on the surface for centuries, benefiting from the Reds' forced labor. After surviving his own execution, Darrow is tasked with a secret mission that will help a rising rebel group: infiltrate the Golds' elite Institute, where the higher-class teenagers are pitted against each other in a brutal war game.

Pierce Brown, the book's author, told The New York Times he was "inspired by the plight of Irish immigrants in the 19th century and by the disenfranchisement of working classes" when writing his dystopian science fiction series. The books that continue this saga are more violent than The Hunger Games, but are a great place to go after Collins' work.

Imagine a race with no finish line, in which failure means death. The Long Walk brings the reader into an imagined authoritarian United States. Every year, the regime supervises a competition which forces 100 boys to walk at a minimum speed of 4 miles per hour. Any person who falls below this speed four times is killed, until there is only one person left. The last boy standing wins the Prize: anything he wants.

Stephen King wrote The Long Walk when he was still a freshman at the University of Maine, and published it under his pseudonym Richard Bachman in July 1979. The Long Walk and Sunrise on the Reaping have more in common than one might think. For one, their two movie adaptations were directed by the same person, Francis Lawrence. However, this story is much more spare and unforgiving. There is little plot and no wide rebellion arc. The story is, instead, focused on the bonds between the boys and the impact of authoritarianism on their lives.

Inesa's mother is in debt. Immensely in debt. So much so that she has signed her 17-year-old daughter up for the Lamb's Gauntlet, a livestreamed 13-day hunt in which a debtor's "Lamb" is pursued across the wasteland by an engineered assassin called an Angel. The competition is run by Caerus, the corporation that controls all aspects of a society built on apocalyptic wastelands. Inesa feels despair at learning the news, but trusts that her hunter brother will help her survive. That is, until she meets the girl tasked with killing her: Melinoë, an experienced assassin desperate to redeem herself after breaking down on camera during her last mission.

The blurb for Fable for the End of the World describes it as "The Last of Us meets The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," and it could not be more accurate. Ava Reid's novel is the closest thing to a Hunger Games story, with a sapphic romance that one can find in a bookshop. Two elements make the story completely unique: its romance between hunter and hunted, and the alternation of their perspectives. Inesa and Melinoë’s growing feelings for each other turn a death match into an enemies-to-lovers romance, while reflecting on the failures of a system that punishes poverty with death.

A group of junior high students is preparing for a field trip. The group includes rock star-to-be Shuya Nanahara; beautiful Mitsuko Souma; transfer student Shogo Kawada; and sociopathic prodigy Kazuo Kiriyama. They live in a fictional 1997 fascist Japan. Its authoritarian government has established the Battle Experiment No. 68 Program, a military program where young students are kidnapped and forced to kill each other until only one remains. The government claims it is research into survival skills and battle readiness, but the population knows the fear it creates is a useful method of control.

Suzanne Collins said she had never heard of Koushun Takami's Battle Royale before writing The Hunger Games. Nonetheless, the two books have a surprising number of elements in common. What sets Takami's story apart is its scale. Instead of focusing on a single point of view, his book follows dozens of students, allowing the reader to get to know their backgrounds and perspectives. Because of this, the world of Battle Royale is much more expansive, and its commentary on military regimes is much more impactful. The deaths are also much more graphic. In 2000, one year after publication, Battle Royale was adapted into a manga series, written by Takami himself, and a feature film.

#3409. ‘Odyssey’ Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema Was More Interested in the Intimate Than the Epic

Christopher Nolan‘s adaptation of Homer’s “The Odyssey” was one of the most awe-inspiring cinematic achievements of 2026, an epic worthy of comparison with the grandiose visions of David Lean and Stanley Kubrick. Yet what interested cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema was less the story’s vast scale than the details of the human faces inhabiting the film‘s sweeping vistas.

“We never really treated it in an epic way,” van Hoytema told IndieWire. “Even though we all know ‘The Odyssey‘ and understand the scale of the story, making some sort of a tourist film was never on our agenda. It was the characters and the visceral sense of their experience that we were interested in, so even standing in the most crazy places in the world — on mountaintops or wherever — we were never motivated by the landscapes. The settings take care of creating the scale and scope of the film — our perspective on the story was a very intimate one.” Related Stories Forget Photorealism: How ‘Wildwood’ Made Its Handmade Digital Artistry Visible ‘Cliff Booth’ Brings Back a Fan-Favorite ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ Face

Given that, van Hoytema tried not to be seduced by the beauty of his surroundings if it didn’t serve the emotional experience. “It was less about showing how beautiful a beach was than about showing how shitty those men felt when they were on the beach,” he said, noting that a key tool in getting across the characters’ internal feelings was shooting the film entirely in IMAX.

“Shooting an entire film in IMAX has been a pursuit of ours for quite a long time now, and we’ve been tweaking the lenses and tweaking the cameras in order to get there,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve managed to wrangle the equipment and technology around it to enable us to be right there next to you, looking straight into your eyes.”

This again plays into that idea of intimacy versus scale, which was something van Hoytema and Nolan had experimented with in “Oppenheimer.” In that film, IMAX was used not only for major set pieces like the atomic bomb test, but quiet dialogue scenes shot largely in close-up. Van Hoytema says that he and Nolan have long been aware that IMAX has historically been used mostly to depict the wonders of the world, but they wanted to expand its grammar.

“The lenses that we use today are an evolution of different iterations of lenses that we have been building through the years, lenses that focus extremely close and that can open wide so that you can work with natural light or in half-darkness,” van Hoytema said. “We’ve found that IMAX is an intimate format because it’s such a good replicator of the human experience and perspective.”

The biggest obstacle toward shooting an entire movie in IMAX before “The Odyssey” was always the sound — IMAX film cameras are famously noisy, making it difficult to get decent production recordings. “We built a blimp on ‘Tenet,’ but it didn’t work,” van Hoytema said. “This was the first film where we felt that the technology had gotten far enough to actually shoot the entire thing on IMAX. There’s been an evolution in development not only in my department but in the sound department — they have come up with better microphones, better filtration, and in this film it came together beautifully.”

Van Hoytema and Nolan always had a backup plan in case the IMAX cameras became too unwieldy or got in the way of performance, particularly in lengthy dialogue scenes that would outlast the cameras’ short magazines. Once Matt Damon and Anne Hathaway proved that they could pull off a complicated sequence in close collaboration with van Hoytema and the other departments, however, Nolan and his crew were confident they could rely on IMAX as their format of choice. “That day was the hardest, and we shot everything on IMAX, so for the rest of the film we just committed — no plan B,” van Hoytema said.

While van Hoytema and Nolan were enthusiastic about committing to IMAX, it did create massive logistical challenges — not just when it came to getting the heavy camera and blimp in and out of remote locations, but in terms of performance. The actors’ eyelines, for example, were often blocked by the enormous camera. “Here we are bragging about the intimacy we can achieve, and suddenly you’re on set with a gigantic black box in front of the actors, and they can’t look each other in the eyes,” van Hoytema said. “It was a huge problem.”

To solve the problem, van Hoytema and his crew built a system that would allow the actors to see each other. “It was based on a teleprompter that has an angled mirror in front of the lens, and people can look straight into the lens reading a teleprompter because it has projected text on it. But instead of text, we had another mirror, and we had an actor sitting here. So basically what actors see is a little surface with a mirror with the other actor in there, and they can look straight into the other actor’s eye.”

Van Hoytema could fine-tune the eyelines by adjusting the angles of the mirrors in what he called “a very analog but very effective solution. And the actors loved it, because instead of looking at a wall they’re literally looking at their co-stars.” Van Hoytema reiterated the idea that everything in the movie was geared toward character and performance — including, at times, making the actors as uncomfortable as possible.

“It’s not for nothing that Chris loves to go out at sea with a ship and do things that are almost physically impossible,” van Hoytema said. “The more miserable or real or wet the situation is, the more the actors have to react to and play with. And that also goes for my way of working. I love different weather situations. I love different light situations. I love kinetic and physical challenges. It adds something unexpected and something visceral. The camera’s always fighting something and the actors are fighting at that very same moment, so it becomes a weirdly symbiotic relationship to the elements.”

In spite — or perhaps because — of the arduous shoot, van Hoytema didn’t want to see it end. “This was an extremely difficult film, but it was also the film where everything we’d been working toward came together,” van Hoytema. “We were much more light-footed. Weirdly enough, when what you’re doing becomes subjected to elements that you cannot control, you become a bit less precious. And that lack of preciousness is very liberating. We just went in headfirst.”

#3407. Netflix's 12-Minute Sci-Fi Short Is So Good, Everyone Should Watch It At Least Once

Netflix has plenty of shows that are often labeled as essential viewing, depending on who is making the recommendation. Few, however, earn that description quite like Love, Death & Robots. Created by Tim Miller, the four-volume series initially looks like yet another animated sci-fi anthology with a particularly generous appetite for violence. Watch a little longer, however, and the true scale of its ambition becomes clear. When LD+R is at its best, these surreal, vibrant shorts blur the boundary between popular entertainment and art.

There are dozens of Love, Death & Robots episodes that need to be seen to be believed, and their strengths vary enormously. Some are emotionally devastating in ways that rival most prestige dramas, while others dive into concepts so abstract and bizarre that it’s amazing they even work as coherent stories. Even among such extraordinary company, though, one LD+R episode demands particular attention. First season standout “The Witness” packs an astonishing amount into just 12 minutes, delivering a viewing experience unlike almost anything else ever put to screen.

“The Witness” is the story of an unnamed woman (voiced by Emily O’Brien) who witnesses a murder and flees through a surreal city, only to find her pursued by the man responsible (Ben Sullivan). Thanks to a time loop, what begins as a frantic escape becomes something far stranger, eventually revealing itself to be a deep reflection on the nature of fear, perception, and violence repeating itself. If anything in Netflix’s library deserves the essential viewing label, this single episode of Love, Death & Robots makes an exceptionally convincing case for it.

Calling “The Witness” one of the best Love, Death & Robots episodes is easy. Justifying the fact that it’s essential television requires more justification. Fortunately, its reputation has some substantial support beyond enthusiastic recommendations from LD+R fans. In 2019, the short won three Emmys: Outstanding Short Form Animated Program, plus individual achievement awards for Alberto Mielgo’s production design and David Pate’s character animation. Its deserved success in these categories neatly reflects its greatest strength: extraordinary visual craftsmanship serving an equally accomplished piece of storytelling.

The production design award makes immediate sense, as “The Witness” is visually stunning even by Love, Death & Robots standards. Buildings, interiors, and crowded streets combine convincing physical detail with rough, painting-like textures, creating somewhere that feels simultaneously grounded and dreamlike. Neon colors make the city seductive, while cramped spaces and disorienting perspectives turn it threatening. Mielgo’s team combined painted backgrounds with keyframed character animation, achieving movement so convincing that viewers questioned whether live action or motion capture had been involved.

Crucially, this spellbinding animation makes the chase at the center of “The Witness” even more gripping. Frantic breathing, awkward trips and fumbles, and frightened expressions give the pursuit an uncomfortable physical immediacy. The animation can exaggerate panic without ever feeling cartoonish. Meanwhile, the masterful editing keeps information just beyond reach. Viewers understand enough to feel the danger, but never enough to assume they know exactly what’s happening until the final, satisfying reveal.

Speaking of, the ending of “The Witness” gives the story a second life. Details that initially register as atmosphere or confusion suddenly invite closer attention, making an immediate rewatch enormously rewarding. There is no heavy-handed last-minute exposition to drain the ending of its power, either. Even for viewers with no intention of exploring the entire Love, Death & Robots anthology, "The Witness" works as an outstanding animated short movie in its own right. It’s visually distinctive, tightly constructed, and remarkably difficult to forget.

“The Witness” is an achievement when it comes to both animation and short-form storytelling. However, that does not automatically make it the definitive Love, Death & Robots episode. Its frantic pacing, explicit imagery, and deliberate ambiguity will appeal more strongly to some viewers than others. What’s more, fans who favor another installment are hardly short of other Love, Death & Robots episodes that make convincing arguments for being the show’s absolute best.

LD+R season 3’s “Jibaro,” also written and directed by Mielgo, is perhaps its strongest rival for sheer visual impact. Its encounter between a deaf knight and a deadly siren becomes a violent exploration of greed and exploitation. Where “The Witness” draws viewers into a pulse-pounding urban pursuit, “Jibaro” uses dance, jagged movement, and startling shifts in sound to create something closer to a tightly choreographed nightmare. It also won the Emmy for Outstanding Short Form Animated Program, in 2022.

For viewers seeking emotional depth, it’s easy to argue that the peak of Love, Death & Robots is season 1’s “Zima Blue”. Its restrained storytelling turns an artist’s search for meaning into a moving reflection on what it means to be human and how much difference there truly is between organic and artificial intelligence. Then there’s “Beyond the Aquila Rift,” which is one of the most chilling cosmic horror stories to ever grace screens. Both can leave a stronger emotional aftereffect than “The Witness,” depending on whether a viewer responds most to quiet revelation, existential terror, or the immediate rush of a chase.

Ultimately, those differences are central to the core appeal of Love, Death & Robots, which has always been its variety. Still, it’s hard to argue against "The Witness" deserving its place among the series’ most celebrated installments, even if it’s not at the absolute top of a fan’s personal ranking. Its clear initial premise makes it accessible, while its visual invention and unnerving payoff make it truly unforgettable. As an introduction to the wider Love, Death & Robots experience, there are few better choices.

#3406. Elizabeth Holmes' Partner Billy Evans Makes Thanksgiving Plea for Her Release

Elizabeth Holmes' partner Billy Evans is making a plea for her release, pointing out their kids have essentially never had Thanksgiving at home with their mother ... and he says there's no rational reason for them to miss another one.

Billy explained his thinking with an emotional post Thursday evening ... which marked the 4th Thanksgiving Elizabeth has been in federal prison for fraud. When she went in, their son was 1 and their daughter was just 3 months, and he asks ... "Who benefits from taking another year of their childhood away from them? How much good could she do with her freedom?"

Billy's really taking umbrage here with the length of Holmes' sentence as a nonviolent criminal -- as he puts it, "She was acquitted of every charge related to patients. Investors themselves acknowledged that their losses caused them no financial hardship."

TBH, he's been ringing this bell ever since Holmes was sentenced. The only thing that's really different now is the renewed attention her case is getting due to Nathan Fielder's documentary, "You Can See Everything" ... which is a frontrunner for a bunch of Oscar nominations.

As you know, Holmes was sentenced to more than 11 years behind bars for defrauding Theranos investors, but Billy's point is ... since she wasn't convicted for harming potential Theranos patients, why is she doing so much time?

Holmes was found guilty of one count of conspiracy to commit fraud on investors, and 3 counts of committing fraud on individual investors ... involving wire transfers of more than $140 million. In other words, white collar crimes.

"You Can See Everything" follows Holmes and her family in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment in 2023, and it's expected to get a Best Picture nomination ... which is extremely rare for a documentary.

We got to chat with Billy on "TMZ Live" ... where he insists he had no idea who the Theranos founder was when they first met, and stood by his partner for her response to the head-scratching "Who's On First?" scene in the doc.

Now, he's hoping the momentum of the film, and the emotions of the holiday season will create more sympathy for Elizabeth. He says, "I would give anything to have her beside us at the table today."

#3402. Before The Lord of the Rings, Tolkien Wrote an Epic Christmas Saga for His Kids

When J.R.R. Tolkien first comes to mind, Middle-earth soon follows. The literary genius who crafted The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings is easily best known for his medieval-inspired work of high fantasy that wove everything from his personal experience during the Great War to his devoted Christian faith into one cohesive mythological tapestry.

However, sometime after he returned home and before he ever published his first novel, Tolkien spun fantastical tales to his children every holiday season leading up to Christmas, which would eventually be collected by his future daughter-in-law, editor Baillie Tolkien, in The Father Christmas Letters, published originally in 1976. Aside from showing another side to Tolkien, the letters also feature some ideas that would later shape Middle-earth.

As noted in the introduction to The Letters from Father Christmas, Tolkien's tradition of annual correspondence from the North Pole began in 1920 when the professor, under the guise of the holiday icon, sent his first letter to his oldest son, John. This continued as Tolkien and his wife, Edith, welcomed more children into their home throughout the decade, as Michael, Christopher, and Priscilla were eventually born. That first letter was quite brief but opened the door to the winter wonderland that Tolkien envisioned. Dated the 22nd of December, Father Christmas — who is later revealed to age with the holiday itself, and is as old as the very first Christmas in Bethlehem — sent Tolkien's eldest son a brief letter with artwork included (a colorful self-portrait and an image of his home in the North Pole). Of course, as the letters progress, more detail is added.

With each year, Father Christmas sent his regards to the children, and with each year, Tolkien infused letters with more hijinks and adventures than the last. The titular figure's own perspective is often juxtaposed with that of the North Polar Bear (also called the Great Polar Bear), his long-time friend and bumbling assistant, as well as his well-written Elven secretary, Ilbereth. Of course, other characters soon followed, as Tolkien expanded the rich, holiday mythology with North Polar Bear's nephews, the "Rory Bory Aylis" fireworks, the presence of Goblins, living snowmen, Red Elves, the Cliff House, and many other unique additions that enhance these glimpses into the love and care the author put into every one of his stories — even those he never thought the world would see.

What began decades earlier as a fun tradition between the professor and his children eventually concluded in 1943 with a final letter penned to his youngest child and only daughter, Priscilla. Here, Father Christmas and the North Polar Bear bid her farewell near the decline of the Second World War, not because they were going away, but because it was time for the tradition to end. Indeed, events from the war itself spill over into the final few letters, with Father Christmas even noting that the Goblins believed the conflict was enough cover to capture the North Pole — though they had not counted on Father Christmas' "Windbeam" and great number of allies. Tolkien used the battle as cover to explain why certain presents and stocking-stuffers did not end up in the Tolkien home on Christmas morning.

Of course, anyone familiar with Tolkien's work can see how some of the worldbuilding aspects of The Father Christmas Letters carried over into his larger legendarium. For one thing, he includes not only Elves and Goblins (as well as a reference to an Elven language), but also "The Man on the Moon," a folktale noted in The Fellowship of the Ring and other Tolkien works. Since The Hobbit itself was published in 1937, it's likely that Tolkien may have worked out some of these ideas in these letters before fastening them to his copy. Indeed, after the release of the novel, he further expands on the conflicts between the North Pole and the Goblin threat, though it could have just as easily had more to do with World War II than any connections to Middle-earth.

One might even go a step further with the influence of Tolkien's Father Christmas epic — which also dabbled in the same sort of rhythmic, poetic material one would find in The Lord of the Rings — on the world of fantasy at large. Of course, Tolkien wasn't the only one to connect the world of Christmas with the fantastical traditions of fairy tales and folklore. The Wizard of Oz author L. Frank Baum had already done so in his 1902 novel, The Life and Adventures of Santa Claus. Yet, Tolkien's efforts for his children may have had an effect on his longtime friend and fellow Inklings member C.S. Lewis. Although we do not know for certain if Lewis was at all privy to any of these letters, we do know that the author saw in Father Christmas the same sort of heroic, charitable, and iconic traits. So, just as he utilized Tolkien's invention of Númenor in his 1945 novel That Hideous Strength, so too did he put Father Christmas in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe in 1950.

But Tolkien cared deeply about Father Christmas, and was quite careful regarding the way he portrayed the mythic holiday figure. According to George Sayer in his book Jack: A Life of C.S. Lewis, Tolkien detested The Chronicles of Narnia for Lewis' "careless" collection of different mythologies, pulling together too many ideas from different points of cultural and historical origin. That criticism was especially true regarding the appearance of Father Christmas himself. Tolkien may have been too harsh, but it's difficult to blame a man who spent decades writing Father Christmas tales for his children, which, for the author, recalled a time when they were young and interested in such fantastical adventures. Little did he know, children around the world would enjoy his stories all these years later. With the holidays at hand, there’s no better time to start a new Tolkien-flavored Christmas tradition — after all, who knows what sort of adventures it may inspire?

The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe is available for streaming on Disney+, and The Lord of the Rings trilogy is available for streaming on HBO Max.

#3394. Jon Bernthal’s 132-Minute Crime Thriller 'The Accountant 2' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Hulu

It can’t always be award-winning dramas and true-crime documentaries when you’re watching movies at home. Sometimes, you want an entertaining, bullet-riddled rollercoaster, and there are few that fit the bill better than 2025’s The Accountant 2. In the long-awaited sequel to the 2016 original, Ben Affleck returns as Christian Wolff, a neurodivergent accountant and trained killer who comes out of hiding to solve a case involving the death of an old friend, which forces him to reunite with his estranged brother, played by Jon Bernthal. The pair make for a unique buddy movie pairing, filled with action and withering put-downs that made the movie a hit with audiences. With the film leaving Hulu on December 1, your last chance to watch it streaming is November 30.

When Ray King (J.K. Simmons), Christian’s ally and government contact, is murdered and found with the cryptic message “find the accountant” on his arm, treasury agent Marybeth Medina (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) seeks out Christian for help. Keen to avenge his friend, he links the killings to a large conspiracy involving the disappearance of a family and dangerous criminals. Realizing he can’t do this alone, he contacts his estranged brother Brax (Bernthal) to help him. With a difficult past between them, the siblings reluctantly come together to piece together the clues and find justice.

Part mystery thriller, part buddy cop movie, the film features the two stars taking on a variety of bad guys as well as solving numerous puzzles to find their target. While undoubtedly a traditional action movie, there’s also a fair amount of laughs to be had as the Wolff boys slowly begin to trust each other again.

Much of the fun of this sequel is in watching the brothers try to co-exist, and seeing their seemingly opposite personalities lead to some hilarious clashes. Christian is methodical, controlled, and able to point out the smallest details, despite having difficulties with social interaction. By contrast, Brax is emotional, abrasive, and constantly seeking connection. He bellows where Christian mutters, meaning that as partners and family members, it can be difficult to find common ground.

While a lazier movie might have positioned Christian’s neurodivergence as making him the outsider, the enjoyment comes from neither brother being the wildcard. Both characters’ personalities have their strengths and weaknesses, and as the story progresses, there’s a sense of satisfaction in the pair finding out that they may have more in common than they realize. It’s in these interactions where Bernthal becomes the movie’s secret weapon. He has a talent for comedy that might not immediately be obvious given his numerous action-heavy roles, but he's adept at highlighting the ridiculousness of his situation, able to use himself for laughs as well as his co-stars.

The first movie was about uncovering who Christian is, given he has built a life where his footprints are covered and his identity protected. However, The Accountant 2 doesn’t have to do the same amount of digging, making this a movie that can almost immediately dive into the action. With the audience being aware of what Christian is capable of, there’s a shorthand that allows the plot to move forward in a swifter way, and gives him a literal brother in arms.

With a growing number of villains on their tail, the action scenes are more frequent, and evolve as the brothers’ relationship becomes stronger. Christian treats all things in life like an equation, with physical altercations being no different. On the other hand, Brax operates on instinct, able to react and change course depending on what the situation calls for. These two approaches slowly begin to complement each other, leading to a terrific finale where they penetrate a heavily armed compound, outnumbered but never outsmarted.

The Accountant 2 moves the formula of the first movie forward in a way that will satisfy fans who want to see more of what they liked from before, but with the volume turned up. WriterBill Dubuque revealed this year that the film’s central pairing was so successful, that there is interest in a third movie focusing on a road trip between Christian and Brax. If that sounds like something you’d be excited about, make sure you catch their latest adventure before it leaves your Hulu menu.

#3391. iOS 27.2 upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27, but the recent release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And in iOS 27.2, Apple introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#3389. Apple Pay just got even better with four new features and more

Apple Pay is a go-to feature for iPhone users when shopping in stores, online, and in apps. Apple recently announced four new features that make Apple Pay even better. Here’s how they work, plus one major expansion that’s rolling out now.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

One of my favorite changes in iOS 27 is the redesigned Apple Pay checkout interface. The new interface makes it much easier to switch between different cards during the checkout flow on websites and in apps.

In the new design, you can easily swipe between cards on the main Apple Pay checkout screen. You can also tap on a card to view a grid of all your available Apple Pay cards.

The design also makes it easier to see information about individual cards, including rewards, balances, pay later options, and more.

iOS 27 was released to everyone last week. You can update in the Settings app on your iPhone.

Apple and American Express recently announced a new partnership that lets you pay with American Express rewards points.

When shopping online or in apps with an American Express card, you’ll see a new “Use Rewards” option alongside your available Membership Rewards points balance. You can apply points to cover all or part of your purchase, right in the Apple Pay checkout flow.

American Express points redeemed via Apple Pay are valued at 0.7 cents each. For example, this means 10,000 points can be redeemed for $70 applied towards your purchase.

In iOS 27, Apple is adding a new “Tap to Share” feature that integrates with Apple Pay on iPhone for in-store shopping.

This feature is an extension of Tap to Pay on iPhone. Apple explains:

With just a tap, customers can connect to a participating merchant’s iPhone for a more personalized and faster in-store purchase experience that allows for secure sharing of information, such as email and other contact information, shipping address, loyalty rewards information, and more.

Customers will also be able to view the items in their basket in real time so they can keep track of what they’ve purchased and ensure all sales and discounts are properly applied.

When done, shoppers can complete the checkout on their iPhone using Apple Pay.

iPhone users with select banks can manage their debit card balances directly in the Apple Pay interface. According to Apple, you’ll be able to use Apple Pay to add money to a supported debit card directly in Apple Wallet or when checking out.

This one isn’t really a new feature developed by Apple. Instead, it’s something that should’ve happened years ago finally coming to fruition. Walmart has announced that it is finally starting to roll out support for Apple Pay. Apple Pay is also rolling out to Sam’s Club as part of this initiative.

As of November, Walmart’s roll out of Apple Pay across the United States is complete.

As Apple Pay continues to increase in popularity and prevalence among retailers, it’s great to see Apple continue to improve the experience. Personally, Apple Pay is my checkout payment method of choice basically everywhere I shop — whether that’s online or in store.

How often do you use Apple Pay? What are your favorite Apple Pay features? Let us know down in the comments.

#3387. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

#3385. 34 Years Later, Clint Eastwood's Best Quote Is Still the Greatest in Western Movie History

For many who grew up in the 1990s, Unforgiven was the definitive Western. It somehow smelled of whiskey, gunsmoke, and a father's aftershave, and remained a monolithic genre presence for years to come — that's how praised it was and how ubiquitous it became on network television after its release. While director, producer, composer, and star Clint Eastwood actually waffled on making the film for years, once he did, he defined the modern revisionist Western and reminded audiences of his incredible talent, while looking back at his career with clear eyes.

Eastwood's last true Western proved to be arguably his finest, while also brutally reassessing the bloodthirsty and heroic clichés he'd embodied for decades. Unforgiven is one of the most melancholic Westerns ever made outside of Italy, and Eastwood's character is given multiple lines and moments when it's clear he's both delivering the character's dialogue and speaking directly to the violence that defined his cinematic career. And while the film is replete with unforgettable moments, his exchange with a naive aspiring gunslinger is arguably the final word on the life of a gunslinger and the genre itself.

In a film full of heartbreaking moments (aided in no small part by Eastwood and Lennie Niehaus's guitar-forward score), few make such an elemental impression as Eastwood's former gunslinger William Munny consoling the brash but inexperienced "Schofield Kid" (Jaimz Woolvett) after he makes his first kill. The Kid has been bragging for half the film about how many men he's shot down, but after Munny presses him into basically executing a man in an outhouse as they chase a bounty, the Kid breaks down. This was his first.

Whiskey and self-reassurance that it's "like it was in the old days," imagining Munny's former profession as romantically as he can, are all the Kid has to hold it together. Eastwood just stares out at the town of Big Whiskey, where he knows there's still killing to be done, and tells him to just take another drink.

"It don't seem real — how you can never breathe again, never. How he's dead ... all on account of pulling a trigger," the Kid breaks down. "It's a hell of a thing, killing a man. Take away all he's got and all he's ever gonna have," Munny replies. And when the Kid insists that their victims "had it coming," Munny just adds: "We all got it coming, kid."

These flicks will entertain just about anybody.

After his spaghetti Western period, with all its stylish, bloodthirsty trappings, and even his own 1973 film High Plains Drifter (in which Eastwood allowed himself to be a quasi-supernatural rapist and mass murderer), Unforgiven can't help but feel like a pause and a look back. It's Eastwood saying goodbye to the genre he remade in his image and reckoning with the fascistic, wanton killing that defined the films that made him Hollywood royalty. Goodbye, Man With No Name and goodbye, Dirty Harry. It's no coincidence that Eastwood would move into a much more classicist auteur phase with his later films, and engage openly and poignantly on topics from the early (and ongoing) sins of the FBI to the horror of the ordinary Japanese soldier at Iwo Jima.

It doesn't hurt that Unforgiven is also a visual and technical masterpiece, with Eastwood genuinely syncing his onscreen persona with his role as director; not a shot is wasted and everything reeks of regret. The film is a widescreen masterpiece that uses weather to its greatest effect. Gene Hackman may ham it up a bit with the cruelty of Munny's target, Little Bill, making it genuinely chilling when he mixes his folksy affect with sudden violence — but when he begs Munny for his life, insisting that he really just wanted to keep building his house, it's as sad as a villain's end can get.

Unforgiven earned Eastwood four well-deserved Oscars, and it hasn't aged a day. While his vast cinematic output is full of certified bangers even in 2026, there's nothing that hits quite as hard as his first true look back on things. Even modern Western masterpieces like the Coen Brothers' beautifully constructed, hilarious and heartbreaking take on True Grit don't have the same weathered soul to them and don't pierce the heart the same way. Eastwood's last word on the genre proved to be just that for all of us.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3378. Two billion credentials publicly exposed, including everything needed for identity theft

A security researcher has discovered a publicly exposed database containing approximately two billion credentials. The database was neither password-protected nor encrypted.

The scariest part of it is around 400,000 documents came from separate folders for individual victims, creating a detailed profile with all the personal data needed to “own that person” …

Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler says that the database contains a huge array of information, including login details for Tor .onion addresses used to access the dark web.

I also observed thousands of Tor .onion addresses associated with account names and passwords. The Tor .onion services are generally categorized as part of the dark web, and these credentials could potentially provide access to private forums, marketplaces, communication platforms, or other hidden services. While .onion accounts alone do not imply criminal or malicious activity, it is estimated that as much as 60% of dark web sites host illegal material and illicit activities. This is the first time I have seen a large number of dark web accounts in breached credentials. It should be noted that legitimate organizations, journalists, whistleblower platforms, and news organizations also operate .onion services to provide anonymity and bypass censorship.

But the most frightening aspect of it is separate folders for individual victims containing all of the information needed for identity theft.

Fowler told Wired that this data appears to have been obtained through advanced malware.

The “scariest” thing in the database, Fowler says, was around 400,000 documents that appeared to come from “more advanced malware” compiling information about individual victims […] that create a detailed profile of an individual and their digital life. “If you had that, you own that person,” Fowler says.

There’s no information about the specific sources of the data, but it seems likely to be aggregated from a range of data breaches. Fowler contacted the hosting company to have the database removed, but it’s not known how many people may have had access to it.

The best protection is to use a password manager like Apple’s Passwords app to ensure you have strong, unique passwords for each individual website and service you use, with two-factor authentication enabled wherever possible. When given the choice of 2FA code delivery, you should always opt for an authenticator app rather than a text message to protect yourself against SIM-swap attacks.

Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3373. TIME’s Top 100 Photos of 2026 list includes a shot taken on iPhone 18 Pro

In September, Apple held a photography exhibition in New York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

The essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

Chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition)

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

“The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

The exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

#3371. CAD images suggest iPhone 18e will have an odd new camera design

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, said to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau …

The iPhone 17e was launched in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

The current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but says that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

#3368. iPhone Handoff: Here’s the latest on carrier availability and pricing

iPhone Handoff is a new feature in iOS 27 that lets you use the same phone number across two different iPhones. However, the feature requires carrier support, so it isn’t available to everyone. Here are the carriers that currently support iPhone Handoff and those that have promised support.

9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

Simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

The biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. Currently, just three carriers support the feature:

What about carriers that are working on the feature? In the United States, Verizon has promised it “will support iPhone Handoff,” but it’s unclear when the feature will launch. Verizon says it will charge $10 per month for the service.

AT&T, meanwhile, has no plans to support iPhone Handoff. In a statement in September, the carrier said that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how quickly the feature will expand around the world.

In my testing, iPhone Handoff works really well. I have it set up between my iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. I use the iPhone Duo 90% of the time, but when I do pick up my iPhone 18 Pro, my number instantly switches to it. There’s a cute animation that expands from the Dynamic Island, confirming that the number has moved.

Have you tried iPhone Handoff? Are you willing to pay extra for it? Let us know down in the comments.

#3365. Muse safety debate continues as the AI agent rolls out in the UK

The debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents …

Meta yesterday announced the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that users are in control and must approve important actions. The company has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but says other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

#3362. iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

#3358. iOS 27 adds new Messages app setting I instantly started using

iOS 27 brought several new features to the Messages app, including a setting that’s long been a popular request: the ability to customize or turn off the audio button. Here’s how to use it.

With iOS 27, Apple fixed a lot of bugs and also granted many feature requests from over the years.

Siri AI is the biggest example of that, offering a big upgrade over the old Siri. But smaller changes in apps like Calendar, Mail, and Messages reflect this focus on wish fulfillment.

In Messages, there’s a new setting that I instantly starting using. It lets you turn off the audio button that normally lives on the right side of the text input field.

The audio button has been conveniently accessible there for years, but I never use it. I don’t think I’ve ever sent an audio message. Sometimes I use dictation, but that’s always available from the bottom-right of the keyboard.

Since I never need that button, the only time it gets pressed is by accident. And as I suspect a lot of users have encountered—including Justin Bieber—it’s very easy to hit by accident.

Thankfully, iOS 27 has the fix. To disable the audio button, follow these steps:

Even if you turn the audio button off, you can still send audio messages by hitting the + button to open your iMessage apps then selecting ‘Audio.’

If you prefer to keep the button active, you can alternately now select ‘Record Audio’ or ‘Start Dictation’ as its function. That way the button will always stay set to your preference instead of dynamically changing like it did before.

#3355. iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

Apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

The iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

The iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

The biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

The iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

The iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.
